nominalTarget.label: Reported target
nominalTarget.scope: Material identity; per-specimen phase and morphology remain separately qualified.

intuition.title: Ligand addition controls nucleation and growth
intuition.text: Oleic acid before tin injection inhibits nucleation. The authors attribute this to strong tin-oleate binding, which lowers the nucleation driving force. Introducing oleic acid after precursor mixing accelerates growth toward an equilibrium size. They report that the final size distribution was independent of the ligand-injection time in their tested series; exact times and Figure S4 remain outside this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Nucleation/growth discussion

intuition.title: Phase character remains qualified
intuition.text: The 175 °C and 105 °C XRD patterns are described as primarily Pnma and Cmcm, respectively. The same discussion warns that peak broadening and similar structures prevent an unambiguous assignment. Figure 1c is a Pnma reference model, not a measured atom-coordinate dataset or proof of a unique 155 °C phase.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figures 1–2 and phase discussion

intuition.title: Particle size is not crystallite size
intuition.text: TEM shows irregular pseudospherical particles and HRTEM shows stacking faults. The authors report that Scherrer grain sizes are typically 30–40% smaller than TEM particle diameters. Figure 3 error bars represent within-sample size distributions, not uncertainty in sample means. Neither the size-series points nor optical gaps are assigned here to an unstated recipe temperature.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, TEM, Scherrer comparison and Figure 3

intuition.title: Surface chemistry produces distinct outcomes
intuition.text: Dodecanethiol displaces oleate and yields a stable suspension; its use during synthesis promotes elongated and branched structures. Ethanedithiol treatment instead immobilizes/crosslinks the NCs, making them insoluble in organic and aqueous solvents. These different operations remain separate; dose, exact conditions and referenced SI images are unavailable in this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Ligand-exchange and modified-growth discussion

intuition.title: Photo-oxidation is an interpretation
intuition.text: Formic-acid-passivated films are photoconductive but show hysteresis and photocurrent degradation. The authors use the energy alignment inferred from cyclic voltammetry to argue that photo-oxidation of surface-bound carboxylic acids likely contributes. This is a source-attributed explanation, not a measured reaction yield or proof that every current change has that origin.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and transport interpretation

intuition.title: Optical confinement has a series-level scope
intuition.text: The source reports 4–10 nm particles and indirect gaps from 0.9 to approximately 1.3 eV, with confinement tapering near 10 nm. Weak emission and a decay faster than the 5 ns instrument response do not establish a resolved fluorescence lifetime or quantum yield. Bulk reference gaps and dielectric constants are literature comparisons rather than measured properties of each prepared sample.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Optical-property discussion

intuition.title: Crystallite, particle and accessible surface are different quantities
intuition.text: The authors associate low BET area in low-water mixtures with sulfate-associated aggregation. Run3 has2.7nm Scherrer crystallites but about10nm TEM particles/aggregates; the reported particle-to-crystallite size ratio is3.7. This does not make the crystallites individually10nm. Runs4–7 surface-area estimates are described as comparable to crystallite size, suggesting single crystals; that is an interpretation, not atomic structural evidence.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.2–3, BET and TEM discussion

intuition.title: Water, alcohol and reflux time affect the reported outcomes
intuition.text: The authors propose that water and higher reflux temperatures favor hydrolysis, while adsorbed alcohol obstructs it. The table retains all individual outcomes, including the nonmonotonic low-water sizes. No unreported mixture boiling temperatures or continuous size predictor are supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main p.2, hydrolysis and solvent discussion

intuition.title: Surface cleaning depends on the treatment
intuition.text: Ammonia washing is associated with sulfate removal and higher surface area. Heating the ammonia-washed product at400°C for1h removes adsorbed ammonia; heating at600°C is associated with sulfate combustion and larger crystallites. The source does not establish that600°C material followed the ammonia/400°C sequence.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.2–3, treatment discussion

intuition.title: Figure2 has conflicting sample numbers
intuition.text: Figure 2 caption labels ammonia-washed panel b as sample 11 and the 400 °C/1 h panel c as sample 12. Table I and the detailed prose instead associate ammonia washing without heating with run 10, ammonia washing plus 400 °C with run 11, and 600 °C with run 12. Both assignments are retained; panels b/c are not treated as unambiguous measurements of any one numbered run.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main p.1 TableI; pp.2–3 treatment prose; p.3 Figure2 caption

intuition.title: Ligand addition controls nucleation and growth
intuition.text: Oleic acid before tin injection inhibits nucleation. The authors attribute this to strong tin-oleate binding, which lowers the nucleation driving force. Introducing oleic acid after precursor mixing accelerates growth toward an equilibrium size. They report that the final size distribution was independent of the ligand-injection time in their tested series; exact times and Figure S4 remain outside this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Nucleation/growth discussion

intuition.title: Phase character remains qualified
intuition.text: The 175 °C and 105 °C XRD patterns are described as primarily Pnma and Cmcm, respectively. The same discussion warns that peak broadening and similar structures prevent an unambiguous assignment. Figure 1c is a Pnma reference model, not a measured atom-coordinate dataset or proof of a unique 155 °C phase.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figures 1–2 and phase discussion

intuition.title: Particle size is not crystallite size
intuition.text: TEM shows irregular pseudospherical particles and HRTEM shows stacking faults. The authors report that Scherrer grain sizes are typically 30–40% smaller than TEM particle diameters. Figure 3 error bars represent within-sample size distributions, not uncertainty in sample means. Neither the size-series points nor optical gaps are assigned here to an unstated recipe temperature.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, TEM, Scherrer comparison and Figure 3

intuition.title: Surface chemistry produces distinct outcomes
intuition.text: Dodecanethiol displaces oleate and yields a stable suspension; its use during synthesis promotes elongated and branched structures. Ethanedithiol treatment instead immobilizes/crosslinks the NCs, making them insoluble in organic and aqueous solvents. These different operations remain separate; dose, exact conditions and referenced SI images are unavailable in this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Ligand-exchange and modified-growth discussion

intuition.title: Photo-oxidation is an interpretation
intuition.text: Formic-acid-passivated films are photoconductive but show hysteresis and photocurrent degradation. The authors use the energy alignment inferred from cyclic voltammetry to argue that photo-oxidation of surface-bound carboxylic acids likely contributes. This is a source-attributed explanation, not a measured reaction yield or proof that every current change has that origin.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and transport interpretation

intuition.title: Optical confinement has a series-level scope
intuition.text: The source reports 4–10 nm particles and indirect gaps from 0.9 to approximately 1.3 eV, with confinement tapering near 10 nm. Weak emission and a decay faster than the 5 ns instrument response do not establish a resolved fluorescence lifetime or quantum yield. Bulk reference gaps and dielectric constants are literature comparisons rather than measured properties of each prepared sample.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Optical-property discussion

intuition.title: Crystallite, particle and accessible surface are different quantities
intuition.text: The authors associate low BET area in low-water mixtures with sulfate-associated aggregation. Run3 has2.7nm Scherrer crystallites but about10nm TEM particles/aggregates; the reported particle-to-crystallite size ratio is3.7. This does not make the crystallites individually10nm. Runs4–7 surface-area estimates are described as comparable to crystallite size, suggesting single crystals; that is an interpretation, not atomic structural evidence.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.2–3, BET and TEM discussion

intuition.title: Water, alcohol and reflux time affect the reported outcomes
intuition.text: The authors propose that water and higher reflux temperatures favor hydrolysis, while adsorbed alcohol obstructs it. The table retains all individual outcomes, including the nonmonotonic low-water sizes. No unreported mixture boiling temperatures or continuous size predictor are supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main p.2, hydrolysis and solvent discussion

intuition.title: Surface cleaning depends on the treatment
intuition.text: Ammonia washing is associated with sulfate removal and higher surface area. Heating the ammonia-washed product at400°C for1h removes adsorbed ammonia; heating at600°C is associated with sulfate combustion and larger crystallites. The source does not establish that600°C material followed the ammonia/400°C sequence.

intuition.title: Surface chemistry produces distinct outcomes
intuition.text: Dodecanethiol displaces oleate and yields a stable suspension; its use during synthesis promotes elongated and branched structures. Ethanedithiol treatment instead immobilizes/crosslinks the NCs, making them insoluble in organic and aqueous solvents. These different operations remain separate; dose, exact conditions and referenced SI images are unavailable in this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Ligand-exchange and modified-growth discussion

intuition.title: Photo-oxidation is an interpretation
intuition.text: Formic-acid-passivated films are photoconductive but show hysteresis and photocurrent degradation. The authors use the energy alignment inferred from cyclic voltammetry to argue that photo-oxidation of surface-bound carboxylic acids likely contributes. This is a source-attributed explanation, not a measured reaction yield or proof that every current change has that origin.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and transport interpretation

intuition.title: Optical confinement has a series-level scope
intuition.text: The source reports 4–10 nm particles and indirect gaps from 0.9 to approximately 1.3 eV, with confinement tapering near 10 nm. Weak emission and a decay faster than the 5 ns instrument response do not establish a resolved fluorescence lifetime or quantum yield. Bulk reference gaps and dielectric constants are literature comparisons rather than measured properties of each prepared sample.

intuition.title: Polymer as growth medium and matrix
intuition.text: The authors grow PbS directly within MEH-PPV, using the polymer as a growth-controlling medium and continuous conductive matrix. They propose steric effects of the polymer chain, rather than charged surfactant groups, as the main growth-control mechanism. Polymer conformation and passivation are not measured atom by atom.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Synthesis concept and growth discussion

intuition.title: Structural scope of the composite
intuition.text: The cleaned material forms a continuous thin composite film containing nonaggregated, polydisperse PbS nanocrystals. The reported average size is4±2nm; the TEM aliquot harvest time is not separately stated. Cubic PbS is identified by selected-area diffraction along[111]. The2µm diffraction area is not a nanocrystal size.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, TEM discussion and Figure1

intuition.title: Optical evidence and alternative explanations
intuition.text: Polymer emission decreases from the pre-injection reference through3- and15-minute samples. The authors interpret this as electronic coupling. They argue that the similar spectral shape accounts for reabsorption and that the lack of a free-ion absorption signature disfavors complex formation, while acknowledging dielectric changes could produce similar effects. No charge-transfer rate or absolute quantum yield is supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figure2 and electronic-coupling discussion

intuition.title: Boundaries of the lifetime and control evidence
intuition.text: The main cites ESI lifetime measurements as further support, but that ESI is not reviewed here. The authors also report bulk PbS without polymer; a separately specified recipe and quantitative control characterization are absent. Neither statement creates an invented additional synthesis–structure row.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, ESI footnote and polymer-free control discussion

intuition.title: Ligand addition controls nucleation and growth
intuition.text: Oleic acid before tin injection inhibits nucleation. The authors attribute this to strong tin-oleate binding, which lowers the nucleation driving force. Introducing oleic acid after precursor mixing accelerates growth toward an equilibrium size. They report that the final size distribution was independent of the ligand-injection time in their tested series; exact times and Figure S4 remain outside this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Nucleation/growth discussion

intuition.title: Phase character remains qualified
intuition.text: The 175 °C and 105 °C XRD patterns are described as primarily Pnma and Cmcm, respectively. The same discussion warns that peak broadening and similar structures prevent an unambiguous assignment. Figure 1c is a Pnma reference model, not a measured atom-coordinate dataset or proof of a unique 155 °C phase.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figures 1–2 and phase discussion

intuition.title: Particle size is not crystallite size
intuition.text: TEM shows irregular pseudospherical particles and HRTEM shows stacking faults. The authors report that Scherrer grain sizes are typically 30–40% smaller than TEM particle diameters. Figure 3 error bars represent within-sample size distributions, not uncertainty in sample means. Neither the size-series points nor optical gaps are assigned here to an unstated recipe temperature.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, TEM, Scherrer comparison and Figure 3

intuition.title: Surface chemistry produces distinct outcomes
intuition.text: Dodecanethiol displaces oleate and yields a stable suspension; its use during synthesis promotes elongated and branched structures. Ethanedithiol treatment instead immobilizes/crosslinks the NCs, making them insoluble in organic and aqueous solvents. These different operations remain separate; dose, exact conditions and referenced SI images are unavailable in this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Ligand-exchange and modified-growth discussion

intuition.title: Photo-oxidation is an interpretation
intuition.text: Formic-acid-passivated films are photoconductive but show hysteresis and photocurrent degradation. The authors use the energy alignment inferred from cyclic voltammetry to argue that photo-oxidation of surface-bound carboxylic acids likely contributes. This is a source-attributed explanation, not a measured reaction yield or proof that every current change has that origin.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and transport interpretation

intuition.title: Optical confinement has a series-level scope
intuition.text: The source reports 4–10 nm particles and indirect gaps from 0.9 to approximately 1.3 eV, with confinement tapering near 10 nm. Weak emission and a decay faster than the 5 ns instrument response do not establish a resolved fluorescence lifetime or quantum yield. Bulk reference gaps and dielectric constants are literature comparisons rather than measured properties of each prepared sample.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Optical-property discussion

intuition.title: Ligand addition controls nucleation and growth
intuition.text: Oleic acid before tin injection inhibits nucleation. The authors attribute this to strong tin-oleate binding, which lowers the nucleation driving force. Introducing oleic acid after precursor mixing accelerates growth toward an equilibrium size. They report that the final size distribution was independent of the ligand-injection time in their tested series; exact times and Figure S4 remain outside this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Nucleation/growth discussion

intuition.title: Phase character remains qualified
intuition.text: The 175 °C and 105 °C XRD patterns are described as primarily Pnma and Cmcm, respectively. The same discussion warns that peak broadening and similar structures prevent an unambiguous assignment. Figure 1c is a Pnma reference model, not a measured atom-coordinate dataset or proof of a unique 155 °C phase.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figures 1–2 and phase discussion

intuition.title: Particle size is not crystallite size
intuition.text: TEM shows irregular pseudospherical particles and HRTEM shows stacking faults. The authors report that Scherrer grain sizes are typically 30–40% smaller than TEM particle diameters. Figure 3 error bars represent within-sample size distributions, not uncertainty in sample means. Neither the size-series points nor optical gaps are assigned here to an unstated recipe temperature.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, TEM, Scherrer comparison and Figure 3

intuition.title: Surface chemistry produces distinct outcomes
intuition.text: Dodecanethiol displaces oleate and yields a stable suspension; its use during synthesis promotes elongated and branched structures. Ethanedithiol treatment instead immobilizes/crosslinks the NCs, making them insoluble in organic and aqueous solvents. These different operations remain separate; dose, exact conditions and referenced SI images are unavailable in this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Ligand-exchange and modified-growth discussion

intuition.title: Photo-oxidation is an interpretation
intuition.text: Formic-acid-passivated films are photoconductive but show hysteresis and photocurrent degradation. The authors use the energy alignment inferred from cyclic voltammetry to argue that photo-oxidation of surface-bound carboxylic acids likely contributes. This is a source-attributed explanation, not a measured reaction yield or proof that every current change has that origin.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and transport interpretation

intuition.title: Optical confinement has a series-level scope
intuition.text: The source reports 4–10 nm particles and indirect gaps from 0.9 to approximately 1.3 eV, with confinement tapering near 10 nm. Weak emission and a decay faster than the 5 ns instrument response do not establish a resolved fluorescence lifetime or quantum yield. Bulk reference gaps and dielectric constants are literature comparisons rather than measured properties of each prepared sample.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Optical-property discussion

intuition.title: Ligand addition controls nucleation and growth
intuition.text: Oleic acid before tin injection inhibits nucleation. The authors attribute this to strong tin-oleate binding, which lowers the nucleation driving force. Introducing oleic acid after precursor mixing accelerates growth toward an equilibrium size. They report that the final size distribution was independent of the ligand-injection time in their tested series; exact times and Figure S4 remain outside this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Nucleation/growth discussion

intuition.title: Phase character remains qualified
intuition.text: The 175 °C and 105 °C XRD patterns are described as primarily Pnma and Cmcm, respectively. The same discussion warns that peak broadening and similar structures prevent an unambiguous assignment. Figure 1c is a Pnma reference model, not a measured atom-coordinate dataset or proof of a unique 155 °C phase.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figures 1–2 and phase discussion

intuition.title: Particle size is not crystallite size
intuition.text: TEM shows irregular pseudospherical particles and HRTEM shows stacking faults. The authors report that Scherrer grain sizes are typically 30–40% smaller than TEM particle diameters. Figure 3 error bars represent within-sample size distributions, not uncertainty in sample means. Neither the size-series points nor optical gaps are assigned here to an unstated recipe temperature.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, TEM, Scherrer comparison and Figure 3

intuition.title: Surface chemistry produces distinct outcomes
intuition.text: Dodecanethiol displaces oleate and yields a stable suspension; its use during synthesis promotes elongated and branched structures. Ethanedithiol treatment instead immobilizes/crosslinks the NCs, making them insoluble in organic and aqueous solvents. These different operations remain separate; dose, exact conditions and referenced SI images are unavailable in this main-only scope.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Ligand-exchange and modified-growth discussion

intuition.title: Photo-oxidation is an interpretation
intuition.text: Formic-acid-passivated films are photoconductive but show hysteresis and photocurrent degradation. The authors use the energy alignment inferred from cyclic voltammetry to argue that photo-oxidation of surface-bound carboxylic acids likely contributes. This is a source-attributed explanation, not a measured reaction yield or proof that every current change has that origin.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and transport interpretation

intuition.title: Optical confinement has a series-level scope
intuition.text: The source reports 4–10 nm particles and indirect gaps from 0.9 to approximately 1.3 eV, with confinement tapering near 10 nm. Weak emission and a decay faster than the 5 ns instrument response do not establish a resolved fluorescence lifetime or quantum yield. Bulk reference gaps and dielectric constants are literature comparisons rather than measured properties of each prepared sample.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Optical-property discussion

intuition.title: Crystallite, particle and accessible surface are different quantities
intuition.text: The authors associate low BET area in low-water mixtures with sulfate-associated aggregation. Run3 has2.7nm Scherrer crystallites but about10nm TEM particles/aggregates; the reported particle-to-crystallite size ratio is3.7. This does not make the crystallites individually10nm. Runs4–7 surface-area estimates are described as comparable to crystallite size, suggesting single crystals; that is an interpretation, not atomic structural evidence.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.2–3, BET and TEM discussion

intuition.title: Water, alcohol and reflux time affect the reported outcomes
intuition.text: The authors propose that water and higher reflux temperatures favor hydrolysis, while adsorbed alcohol obstructs it. The table retains all individual outcomes, including the nonmonotonic low-water sizes. No unreported mixture boiling temperatures or continuous size predictor are supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main p.2, hydrolysis and solvent discussion

intuition.title: Surface cleaning depends on the treatment
intuition.text: Ammonia washing is associated with sulfate removal and higher surface area. Heating the ammonia-washed product at400°C for1h removes adsorbed ammonia; heating at600°C is associated with sulfate combustion and larger crystallites. The source does not establish that600°C material followed the ammonia/400°C sequence.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.2–3, treatment discussion

intuition.title: Figure2 has conflicting sample numbers
intuition.text: Figure 2 caption labels ammonia-washed panel b as sample 11 and the 400 °C/1 h panel c as sample 12. Table I and the detailed prose instead associate ammonia washing without heating with run 10, ammonia washing plus 400 °C with run 11, and 600 °C with run 12. Both assignments are retained; panels b/c are not treated as unambiguous measurements of any one numbered run.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main p.1 TableI; pp.2–3 treatment prose; p.3 Figure2 caption

intuition.title: Polymer as growth medium and matrix
intuition.text: The authors grow PbS directly within MEH-PPV, using the polymer as a growth-controlling medium and continuous conductive matrix. They propose steric effects of the polymer chain, rather than charged surfactant groups, as the main growth-control mechanism. Polymer conformation and passivation are not measured atom by atom.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Synthesis concept and growth discussion

intuition.title: Structural scope of the composite
intuition.text: The cleaned material forms a continuous thin composite film containing nonaggregated, polydisperse PbS nanocrystals. The reported average size is4±2nm; the TEM aliquot harvest time is not separately stated. Cubic PbS is identified by selected-area diffraction along[111]. The2µm diffraction area is not a nanocrystal size.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, TEM discussion and Figure1

intuition.title: Optical evidence and alternative explanations
intuition.text: Polymer emission decreases from the pre-injection reference through3- and15-minute samples. The authors interpret this as electronic coupling. They argue that the similar spectral shape accounts for reabsorption and that the lack of a free-ion absorption signature disfavors complex formation, while acknowledging dielectric changes could produce similar effects. No charge-transfer rate or absolute quantum yield is supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figure2 and electronic-coupling discussion

intuition.title: Boundaries of the lifetime and control evidence
intuition.text: The main cites ESI lifetime measurements as further support, but that ESI is not reviewed here. The authors also report bulk PbS without polymer; a separately specified recipe and quantitative control characterization are absent. Neither statement creates an invented additional synthesis–structure row.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, ESI footnote and polymer-free control discussion

intuition.title: Precursor aggregation persists through treatment
intuition.text: The authors contrast loose initial sols with more strongly aggregated ammonia-precipitated suspensions. Microwave-treated suspension particles remain polydisperse; treated sols have narrower distributions and primarily hexagonal outlines. This is a morphological comparison, not a hexagonal-phase assignment.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.1–3; Figures1–2 and table

intuition.title: Do not merge XRD and microscopy sizes
intuition.text: The table reports coherent-scattering domains separately from TEM averages. Initial rows report XRD <5nm and TEM mean4nm; their prose TEM ranges and optical sol size estimate remain different measurement contexts.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.1–3; equation1 and table

intuition.title: Additional conditions are not a complete matrix
intuition.text: Some experiments extend microwave treatment to6h without a sample-resolved temperature mapping; suspension CSD stays unchanged. The ordinary hydrothermal comparator reports a typical15nm CSD but no complete temperature/time recipe. No additional crossed variants or digitized distribution points are invented.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.1–2

intuition.title: Sintering suitability is a proposal
intuition.text: The authors suggest that narrow distributions and weak interparticle contacts may help low-temperature sintering by limiting irreversible pores and favoring uniform ceramics. No sintering experiment or performance measurement is supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main p.3, conclusion

intuition.title: Sol stability mechanism is proposed
intuition.text: Authors suggest adsorbed hydroxyl ions can stabilize the sol. Prolonged storage lowers pH to5–6 and accompanies coagulation; no storage duration or direct surface-coverage measurement is given.
intuition.source_locator: Main p.1, final paragraph

intuition.title: Precursor aggregation persists through treatment
intuition.text: The authors contrast loose initial sols with more strongly aggregated ammonia-precipitated suspensions. Microwave-treated suspension particles remain polydisperse; treated sols have narrower distributions and primarily hexagonal outlines. This is a morphological comparison, not a hexagonal-phase assignment.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.1–3; Figures1–2 and table

intuition.title: Do not merge XRD and microscopy sizes
intuition.text: The table reports coherent-scattering domains separately from TEM averages. Initial rows report XRD <5nm and TEM mean4nm; their prose TEM ranges and optical sol size estimate remain different measurement contexts.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main pp.1–3; equation1 and table

intuition.title: Additional conditions are not a complete matrix
intuition.text: Some experiments extend microwave treatment to6h without a sample-resolved temperature mapping; suspension CSD stays unchanged. The ordinary hydrothermal comparator reports a typical15nm CSD but no complete temperature/time recipe. No additional crossed variants or digitized distribution points are invented.

intuition.title: Sintering suitability is a proposal
intuition.text: The authors suggest that narrow distributions and weak interparticle contacts may help low-temperature sintering by limiting irreversible pores and favoring uniform ceramics. No sintering experiment or performance measurement is supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied main p.3, conclusion

intuition.title: Sol stability mechanism is proposed
intuition.text: Authors suggest adsorbed hydroxyl ions can stabilize the sol. Prolonged storage lowers pH to5–6 and accompanies coagulation; no storage duration or direct surface-coverage measurement is given.

intuition.title: Compare two acid-specific hydrothermal preparations
intuition.text: The study deliberately changes acid identity, initial pH and hydrothermal temperature to obtain two anatase colloids with similar primary sizes. Sample 1 uses acetic acid at pH 2 and 280 °C; sample 2 uses nitric acid at pH 1.9 and 250 °C. The authors interpret later solution-behavior differences in terms of surface structure; the prior facet study is cited, not independently remeasured here.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, 6, Introduction, Colloid Synthesis and surface discussion

intuition.title: Each size method describes a different object or estimator
intuition.text: TEM reports number-average projected particle dimensions; XRD reports volume-average coherent crystallite sizes. DLS measures solvated, aggregated hydrodynamic dimensions. AUC sizes calculated using bulk anatase density and later hydration-model core sizes are derived interpretations, not interchangeable direct particle measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–5, Figures 1–5 and DLS/model discussion

intuition.title: Analytical pH reveals different aggregation responses
intuition.text: Both samples are already aggregated at pH 1 according to the authors. Sample 2 shows strong aggregation between pH 1.96 and 1.99, whereas sample 1 follows a different sedimentation trend despite similar zeta potentials below the point of zero charge. These pH settings characterize the prepared colloids; they do not create extra synthesis recipe–structure pairs.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–5, Figures 3–5 and DLS block

intuition.title: Hydration shells are a qualified model
intuition.text: The authors combine DLS and AUC under hard-sphere and negligible-charge assumptions to infer an apparent hydrated density. Their spherical anatase-core/water-shell illustration is explicitly inadequate for aggregates, and shape cannot be separated from hydration using AUC alone. The last model row is printed as sample 1 at pH 1.96 although related DLS/density and conclusion statements concern sample 2; the assignment remains unresolved.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 5–6, Equation 4, model list and limitations

intuition.title: A future combined method is not a performed experiment
intuition.text: Flow field-flow fractionation coupled to AUC is proposed as future work to disentangle size, shape, hydration and charge distributions. It is not an additional demonstrated preparation or measurement series in this contribution.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 6, Conclusion

intuition.title: Compare two acid-specific hydrothermal preparations
intuition.text: The study deliberately changes acid identity, initial pH and hydrothermal temperature to obtain two anatase colloids with similar primary sizes. Sample 1 uses acetic acid at pH 2 and 280 °C; sample 2 uses nitric acid at pH 1.9 and 250 °C. The authors interpret later solution-behavior differences in terms of surface structure; the prior facet study is cited, not independently remeasured here.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, 6, Introduction, Colloid Synthesis and surface discussion

intuition.title: Each size method describes a different object or estimator
intuition.text: TEM reports number-average projected particle dimensions; XRD reports volume-average coherent crystallite sizes. DLS measures solvated, aggregated hydrodynamic dimensions. AUC sizes calculated using bulk anatase density and later hydration-model core sizes are derived interpretations, not interchangeable direct particle measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–5, Figures 1–5 and DLS/model discussion

intuition.title: Analytical pH reveals different aggregation responses
intuition.text: Both samples are already aggregated at pH 1 according to the authors. Sample 2 shows strong aggregation between pH 1.96 and 1.99, whereas sample 1 follows a different sedimentation trend despite similar zeta potentials below the point of zero charge. These pH settings characterize the prepared colloids; they do not create extra synthesis recipe–structure pairs.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–5, Figures 3–5 and DLS block

intuition.title: Hydration shells are a qualified model
intuition.text: The authors combine DLS and AUC under hard-sphere and negligible-charge assumptions to infer an apparent hydrated density. Their spherical anatase-core/water-shell illustration is explicitly inadequate for aggregates, and shape cannot be separated from hydration using AUC alone. The last model row is printed as sample 1 at pH 1.96 although related DLS/density and conclusion statements concern sample 2; the assignment remains unresolved.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 5–6, Equation 4, model list and limitations

intuition.title: A future combined method is not a performed experiment
intuition.text: Flow field-flow fractionation coupled to AUC is proposed as future work to disentangle size, shape, hydration and charge distributions. It is not an additional demonstrated preparation or measurement series in this contribution.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 6, Conclusion

intuition.title: Mg feed controls hierarchical morphology
intuition.text: At fixed 20 mM CaCl2, the source reports regular rhombohedra without Mg, elongated rhombohedra at 10–20 mM Mg2+, dumbbells at 40 mM, and stacked spheres over 50–60 mM. The 60 mM images illustrate the latter range; no separately labelled 50 mM batch is invented. At 100 mM, the identified deposit is amorphous calcium carbonate with a smooth planar surface.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 1, 3–4 and morphology discussion

intuition.title: Three structural scales must remain distinct
intuition.text: Macroscopic architectures comprise triangular submicron units, described as several hundred nanometers wide, which contain nanocrystals. At 20 mM, SEM describes nanocrystals smaller than 50 nm and HRTEM resolves 5–20 nm mosaic domains. At 40/60 mM, surface crystallites are reported smaller than 20 nm; the 40 mM fractured radial interior separately contains 20–30 nm crystallites. These observations are not a single averaged particle size.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 4–6 and size descriptions

intuition.title: Mg substitution and excess amorphous material
intuition.text: The (104) calcite peak shifts to higher angle and broadens with Mg feed. Substitution inferred from lattice contraction is lower than total Mg measured by ion chromatography, suggesting Mg outside the crystal lattice. The abstract states ca. 6% maximum substitution; exact per-feed values are only graphed and are not digitized here. The authors propose that excess Mg stabilizes ACC, suppressing regular growth and producing connected nanocrystals; this is a mechanistic interpretation, not a measured growth rate.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–4, Abstract, Figure 2 and mechanism

intuition.title: SI calibration versus product evidence
intuition.text: SI Figure S1 plots reference lattice spacings from database entries for calcite, high-Mg calcite, dolomite and magnesite; these are not new products or measured current unit cells. SI Figure S2 is the source FTIR series at 0, 10, 20, 40 and 100 mM Mg. Its band assignments support calcite versus ACC and water, without turning every listed band into a measured peak for every specimen.
intuition.source_locator: SI PDF p. 1–2, Figures S1–S2

intuition.title: Reported setup and missing duration
intuition.text: Each vessel contains 50 cm3 precursor solution and FTO substrate under a polymer cover with several pinholes. Two vessels share a 750 cm3 desiccator and 4.0 g ammonium carbonate CO2 source at 25 °C. Deposition time, pH, post-treatment, substrate dimensions and pinhole geometry are unreported. The shared carbonate charge is not duplicated into per-vessel charges.

intuition.title: Mg feed controls hierarchical morphology
intuition.text: At fixed 20 mM CaCl2, the source reports regular rhombohedra without Mg, elongated rhombohedra at 10–20 mM Mg2+, dumbbells at 40 mM, and stacked spheres over 50–60 mM. The 60 mM images illustrate the latter range; no separately labelled 50 mM batch is invented. At 100 mM, the identified deposit is amorphous calcium carbonate with a smooth planar surface.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 1, 3–4 and morphology discussion

intuition.title: Three structural scales must remain distinct
intuition.text: Macroscopic architectures comprise triangular submicron units, described as several hundred nanometers wide, which contain nanocrystals. At 20 mM, SEM describes nanocrystals smaller than 50 nm and HRTEM resolves 5–20 nm mosaic domains. At 40/60 mM, surface crystallites are reported smaller than 20 nm; the 40 mM fractured radial interior separately contains 20–30 nm crystallites. These observations are not a single averaged particle size.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 4–6 and size descriptions

intuition.title: Mg substitution and excess amorphous material
intuition.text: The (104) calcite peak shifts to higher angle and broadens with Mg feed. Substitution inferred from lattice contraction is lower than total Mg measured by ion chromatography, suggesting Mg outside the crystal lattice. The abstract states ca. 6% maximum substitution; exact per-feed values are only graphed and are not digitized here. The authors propose that excess Mg stabilizes ACC, suppressing regular growth and producing connected nanocrystals; this is a mechanistic interpretation, not a measured growth rate.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–4, Abstract, Figure 2 and mechanism

intuition.title: SI calibration versus product evidence
intuition.text: SI Figure S1 plots reference lattice spacings from database entries for calcite, high-Mg calcite, dolomite and magnesite; these are not new products or measured current unit cells. SI Figure S2 is the source FTIR series at 0, 10, 20, 40 and 100 mM Mg. Its band assignments support calcite versus ACC and water, without turning every listed band into a measured peak for every specimen.
intuition.source_locator: SI PDF p. 1–2, Figures S1–S2

intuition.title: Reported setup and missing duration
intuition.text: Each vessel contains 50 cm3 precursor solution and FTO substrate under a polymer cover with several pinholes. Two vessels share a 750 cm3 desiccator and 4.0 g ammonium carbonate CO2 source at 25 °C. Deposition time, pH, post-treatment, substrate dimensions and pinhole geometry are unreported. The shared carbonate charge is not duplicated into per-vessel charges.

intuition.title: Mg feed controls hierarchical morphology
intuition.text: At fixed 20 mM CaCl2, the source reports regular rhombohedra without Mg, elongated rhombohedra at 10–20 mM Mg2+, dumbbells at 40 mM, and stacked spheres over 50–60 mM. The 60 mM images illustrate the latter range; no separately labelled 50 mM batch is invented. At 100 mM, the identified deposit is amorphous calcium carbonate with a smooth planar surface.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 1, 3–4 and morphology discussion

intuition.title: Three structural scales must remain distinct
intuition.text: Macroscopic architectures comprise triangular submicron units, described as several hundred nanometers wide, which contain nanocrystals. At 20 mM, SEM describes nanocrystals smaller than 50 nm and HRTEM resolves 5–20 nm mosaic domains. At 40/60 mM, surface crystallites are reported smaller than 20 nm; the 40 mM fractured radial interior separately contains 20–30 nm crystallites. These observations are not a single averaged particle size.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 4–6 and size descriptions

intuition.title: Mg substitution and excess amorphous material
intuition.text: The (104) calcite peak shifts to higher angle and broadens with Mg feed. Substitution inferred from lattice contraction is lower than total Mg measured by ion chromatography, suggesting Mg outside the crystal lattice. The abstract states ca. 6% maximum substitution; exact per-feed values are only graphed and are not digitized here. The authors propose that excess Mg stabilizes ACC, suppressing regular growth and producing connected nanocrystals; this is a mechanistic interpretation, not a measured growth rate.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–4, Abstract, Figure 2 and mechanism

intuition.title: SI calibration versus product evidence
intuition.text: SI Figure S1 plots reference lattice spacings from database entries for calcite, high-Mg calcite, dolomite and magnesite; these are not new products or measured current unit cells. SI Figure S2 is the source FTIR series at 0, 10, 20, 40 and 100 mM Mg. Its band assignments support calcite versus ACC and water, without turning every listed band into a measured peak for every specimen.
intuition.source_locator: SI PDF p. 1–2, Figures S1–S2

intuition.title: Reported setup and missing duration
intuition.text: Each vessel contains 50 cm3 precursor solution and FTO substrate under a polymer cover with several pinholes. Two vessels share a 750 cm3 desiccator and 4.0 g ammonium carbonate CO2 source at 25 °C. Deposition time, pH, post-treatment, substrate dimensions and pinhole geometry are unreported. The shared carbonate charge is not duplicated into per-vessel charges.

intuition.title: Precursor and drying branches
intuition.text: Sol–gel hydrolysis of zirconium n-propoxide and precipitation from zirconium oxychloride are distinct recipes. Each has oven (110 °C, 12 h) and Rotavapor vacuum (70 °C, 50 mbar, duration unreported) drying branches, followed by 400, 500, 600 or 700 °C calcination for 4 h in static air. The four uncalcined states remain separate supporting specimens.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Sections 2.1–2.3 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Sol–gel feed ambiguity is retained
intuition.text: The paper describes purchased 70 wt% zirconium propoxide solution, dilution to 30 wt%, a 0.025 M precursor and a typical charge of 17.7 g Zr-P plus 41.3 g n-propanol. Whether the stated precursor mass denotes stock solution or neat-equivalent reagent is unresolved. No molar charge or corrected concentration is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.2

intuition.title: Phase fractions and domain sizes are separate
intuition.text: Table 1 reports XRD peak-area tetragonal/monoclinic fractions; blank cells and the printed dash do not become inferred zeros. Table 2 gives phase/reflection-specific Scherrer crystallite sizes and lattice strains, not SEM particle diameters. Its strain unit or scale is unspecified. At 700 °C, SG-O is 23 nm in Table 2 but 20 nm in the prose; both are retained with the explicit table used in structured measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3,5–6, Tables 1–2 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Stabilization is an interpretation
intuition.text: The authors relate retention of tetragonal zirconia to small crystallites, hydroxyl groups and lattice strain, with greater thermal stability for sol–gel material. Vacuum drying initially produces larger domains. These explanations and the cited critical-size literature are not additional measured thresholds or current sample recipes. Exact residual tetragonal fractions at high temperature are retained instead of treating summarized complete transformation as zero.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4,6–7, Structural discussion and conclusions

intuition.title: Before-calcination morphology has its own scope
intuition.text: Figure 6 shows spherical sol–gel particles after either drying route. Precipitation gives predominantly cubic/rectangular particles of varying sizes after oven drying, with some spherical particles after vacuum drying. These images are before calcination; no numerical SEM particle mean or automatic post-calcination shape is assigned.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 6–7, Figure 6 and Section 3.4

intuition.title: Textural and thermal measurements
intuition.text: Table 3 reports only before-calcination and 400 °C textural values. Surface areas and pore volumes decrease while average pore diameters increase. Figure 5 shows before-calcination N2 isotherms, interpreted as combined H2/H3 hysteresis with ink-bottle and slit pores. TG/DTG weight loss of 22–33% and mechanisms remain study-level context without exact batch-specific values.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–7, Thermal discussion, Figure 5, Table 3 and Sections 3.2–3.3

intuition.title: Precursor and drying branches
intuition.text: Sol–gel hydrolysis of zirconium n-propoxide and precipitation from zirconium oxychloride are distinct recipes. Each has oven (110 °C, 12 h) and Rotavapor vacuum (70 °C, 50 mbar, duration unreported) drying branches, followed by 400, 500, 600 or 700 °C calcination for 4 h in static air. The four uncalcined states remain separate supporting specimens.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Sections 2.1–2.3 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Sol–gel feed ambiguity is retained
intuition.text: The paper describes purchased 70 wt% zirconium propoxide solution, dilution to 30 wt%, a 0.025 M precursor and a typical charge of 17.7 g Zr-P plus 41.3 g n-propanol. Whether the stated precursor mass denotes stock solution or neat-equivalent reagent is unresolved. No molar charge or corrected concentration is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.2

intuition.title: Phase fractions and domain sizes are separate
intuition.text: Table 1 reports XRD peak-area tetragonal/monoclinic fractions; blank cells and the printed dash do not become inferred zeros. Table 2 gives phase/reflection-specific Scherrer crystallite sizes and lattice strains, not SEM particle diameters. Its strain unit or scale is unspecified. At 700 °C, SG-O is 23 nm in Table 2 but 20 nm in the prose; both are retained with the explicit table used in structured measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3,5–6, Tables 1–2 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Stabilization is an interpretation
intuition.text: The authors relate retention of tetragonal zirconia to small crystallites, hydroxyl groups and lattice strain, with greater thermal stability for sol–gel material. Vacuum drying initially produces larger domains. These explanations and the cited critical-size literature are not additional measured thresholds or current sample recipes. Exact residual tetragonal fractions at high temperature are retained instead of treating summarized complete transformation as zero.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4,6–7, Structural discussion and conclusions

intuition.title: Before-calcination morphology has its own scope
intuition.text: Figure 6 shows spherical sol–gel particles after either drying route. Precipitation gives predominantly cubic/rectangular particles of varying sizes after oven drying, with some spherical particles after vacuum drying. These images are before calcination; no numerical SEM particle mean or automatic post-calcination shape is assigned.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 6–7, Figure 6 and Section 3.4

intuition.title: Textural and thermal measurements
intuition.text: Table 3 reports only before-calcination and 400 °C textural values. Surface areas and pore volumes decrease while average pore diameters increase. Figure 5 shows before-calcination N2 isotherms, interpreted as combined H2/H3 hysteresis with ink-bottle and slit pores. TG/DTG weight loss of 22–33% and mechanisms remain study-level context without exact batch-specific values.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–7, Thermal discussion, Figure 5, Table 3 and Sections 3.2–3.3

intuition.title: Precursor and drying branches
intuition.text: Sol–gel hydrolysis of zirconium n-propoxide and precipitation from zirconium oxychloride are distinct recipes. Each has oven (110 °C, 12 h) and Rotavapor vacuum (70 °C, 50 mbar, duration unreported) drying branches, followed by 400, 500, 600 or 700 °C calcination for 4 h in static air. The four uncalcined states remain separate supporting specimens.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Sections 2.1–2.3 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Sol–gel feed ambiguity is retained
intuition.text: The paper describes purchased 70 wt% zirconium propoxide solution, dilution to 30 wt%, a 0.025 M precursor and a typical charge of 17.7 g Zr-P plus 41.3 g n-propanol. Whether the stated precursor mass denotes stock solution or neat-equivalent reagent is unresolved. No molar charge or corrected concentration is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.2

intuition.title: Phase fractions and domain sizes are separate
intuition.text: Table 1 reports XRD peak-area tetragonal/monoclinic fractions; blank cells and the printed dash do not become inferred zeros. Table 2 gives phase/reflection-specific Scherrer crystallite sizes and lattice strains, not SEM particle diameters. Its strain unit or scale is unspecified. At 700 °C, SG-O is 23 nm in Table 2 but 20 nm in the prose; both are retained with the explicit table used in structured measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3,5–6, Tables 1–2 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Stabilization is an interpretation
intuition.text: The authors relate retention of tetragonal zirconia to small crystallites, hydroxyl groups and lattice strain, with greater thermal stability for sol–gel material. Vacuum drying initially produces larger domains. These explanations and the cited critical-size literature are not additional measured thresholds or current sample recipes. Exact residual tetragonal fractions at high temperature are retained instead of treating summarized complete transformation as zero.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4,6–7, Structural discussion and conclusions

intuition.title: Before-calcination morphology has its own scope
intuition.text: Figure 6 shows spherical sol–gel particles after either drying route. Precipitation gives predominantly cubic/rectangular particles of varying sizes after oven drying, with some spherical particles after vacuum drying. These images are before calcination; no numerical SEM particle mean or automatic post-calcination shape is assigned.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 6–7, Figure 6 and Section 3.4

intuition.title: Textural and thermal measurements
intuition.text: Table 3 reports only before-calcination and 400 °C textural values. Surface areas and pore volumes decrease while average pore diameters increase. Figure 5 shows before-calcination N2 isotherms, interpreted as combined H2/H3 hysteresis with ink-bottle and slit pores. TG/DTG weight loss of 22–33% and mechanisms remain study-level context without exact batch-specific values.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–7, Thermal discussion, Figure 5, Table 3 and Sections 3.2–3.3

intuition.title: Precursor and drying branches
intuition.text: Sol–gel hydrolysis of zirconium n-propoxide and precipitation from zirconium oxychloride are distinct recipes. Each has oven (110 °C, 12 h) and Rotavapor vacuum (70 °C, 50 mbar, duration unreported) drying branches, followed by 400, 500, 600 or 700 °C calcination for 4 h in static air. The four uncalcined states remain separate supporting specimens.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Sections 2.1–2.3 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Sol–gel feed ambiguity is retained
intuition.text: The paper describes purchased 70 wt% zirconium propoxide solution, dilution to 30 wt%, a 0.025 M precursor and a typical charge of 17.7 g Zr-P plus 41.3 g n-propanol. Whether the stated precursor mass denotes stock solution or neat-equivalent reagent is unresolved. No molar charge or corrected concentration is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.2

intuition.title: Phase fractions and domain sizes are separate
intuition.text: Table 1 reports XRD peak-area tetragonal/monoclinic fractions; blank cells and the printed dash do not become inferred zeros. Table 2 gives phase/reflection-specific Scherrer crystallite sizes and lattice strains, not SEM particle diameters. Its strain unit or scale is unspecified. At 700 °C, SG-O is 23 nm in Table 2 but 20 nm in the prose; both are retained with the explicit table used in structured measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3,5–6, Tables 1–2 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Stabilization is an interpretation
intuition.text: The authors relate retention of tetragonal zirconia to small crystallites, hydroxyl groups and lattice strain, with greater thermal stability for sol–gel material. Vacuum drying initially produces larger domains. These explanations and the cited critical-size literature are not additional measured thresholds or current sample recipes. Exact residual tetragonal fractions at high temperature are retained instead of treating summarized complete transformation as zero.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4,6–7, Structural discussion and conclusions

intuition.title: Before-calcination morphology has its own scope
intuition.text: Figure 6 shows spherical sol–gel particles after either drying route. Precipitation gives predominantly cubic/rectangular particles of varying sizes after oven drying, with some spherical particles after vacuum drying. These images are before calcination; no numerical SEM particle mean or automatic post-calcination shape is assigned.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 6–7, Figure 6 and Section 3.4

intuition.title: Textural and thermal measurements
intuition.text: Table 3 reports only before-calcination and 400 °C textural values. Surface areas and pore volumes decrease while average pore diameters increase. Figure 5 shows before-calcination N2 isotherms, interpreted as combined H2/H3 hysteresis with ink-bottle and slit pores. TG/DTG weight loss of 22–33% and mechanisms remain study-level context without exact batch-specific values.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–7, Thermal discussion, Figure 5, Table 3 and Sections 3.2–3.3

intuition.text: The paper describes purchased 70 wt% zirconium propoxide solution, dilution to 30 wt%, a 0.025 M precursor and a typical charge of 17.7 g Zr-P plus 41.3 g n-propanol. Whether the stated precursor mass denotes stock solution or neat-equivalent reagent is unresolved. No molar charge or corrected concentration is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.2

intuition.title: Phase fractions and domain sizes are separate
intuition.text: Table 1 reports XRD peak-area tetragonal/monoclinic fractions; blank cells and the printed dash do not become inferred zeros. intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3,5–6, Tables 1–2 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Stabilization is an interpretation
intuition.text: The authors relate retention of tetragonal zirconia to small crystallites, hydroxyl groups and lattice strain, with greater thermal stability for sol–gel material. Vacuum drying initially produces larger domains. These explanations and the cited critical-size literature are not additional measured thresholds or current sample recipes. Exact residual tetragonal fractions at high temperature are retained instead of treating summarized complete transformation as zero.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4,6–7, Structural discussion and conclusions

intuition.title: Before-calcination morphology has its own scope
intuition.text: Figure 6 shows spherical sol–gel particles after either drying route. Precipitation gives predominantly cubic/rectangular particles of varying sizes after oven drying, with some spherical particles after vacuum drying. These images are before calcination; no numerical SEM particle mean or automatic post-calcination shape is assigned.

intuition.title: Textural and thermal measurements

intuition.title: Precursor and drying branches
intuition.text: Sol–gel hydrolysis of zirconium n-propoxide and precipitation from zirconium oxychloride are distinct recipes. Each has oven (110 °C, 12 h) and Rotavapor vacuum (70 °C, 50 mbar, duration unreported) drying branches, followed by 400, 500, 600 or 700 °C calcination for 4 h in static air. The four uncalcined states remain separate supporting specimens.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Sections 2.1–2.3 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Sol–gel feed ambiguity is retained
intuition.text: The paper describes purchased 70 wt% zirconium propoxide solution, dilution to 30 wt%, a 0.025 M precursor and a typical charge of 17.7 g Zr-P plus 41.3 g n-propanol. Whether the stated precursor mass denotes stock solution or neat-equivalent reagent is unresolved. No molar charge or corrected concentration is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.2

intuition.title: Phase fractions and domain sizes are separate
intuition.text: Table 1 reports XRD peak-area tetragonal/monoclinic fractions; blank cells and the printed dash do not become inferred zeros. Table 2 gives phase/reflection-specific Scherrer crystallite sizes and lattice strains, not SEM particle diameters. Its strain unit or scale is unspecified. At 700 °C, SG-O is 23 nm in Table 2 but 20 nm in the prose; both are retained with the explicit table used in structured measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3,5–6, Tables 1–2 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Stabilization is an interpretation
intuition.text: The authors relate retention of tetragonal zirconia to small crystallites, hydroxyl groups and lattice strain, with greater thermal stability for sol–gel material. Vacuum drying initially produces larger domains. These explanations and the cited critical-size literature are not additional measured thresholds or current sample recipes. Exact residual tetragonal fractions at high temperature are retained instead of treating summarized complete transformation as zero.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4,6–7, Structural discussion and conclusions

intuition.title: Before-calcination morphology has its own scope
intuition.text: Figure 6 shows spherical sol–gel particles after either drying route. Precipitation gives predominantly cubic/rectangular particles of varying sizes after oven drying, with some spherical particles after vacuum drying. These images are before calcination; no numerical SEM particle mean or automatic post-calcination shape is assigned.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 6–7, Figure 6 and Section 3.4

intuition.title: Textural and thermal measurements
intuition.text: Table 3 reports only before-calcination and 400 °C textural values. Surface areas and pore volumes decrease while average pore diameters increase. Figure 5 shows before-calcination N2 isotherms, interpreted as combined H2/H3 hysteresis with ink-bottle and slit pores. TG/DTG weight loss of 22–33% and mechanisms remain study-level context without exact batch-specific values.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–7, Thermal discussion, Figure 5, Table 3 and Sections 3.2–3.3

intuition.title: Precursor and drying branches
intuition.text: Sol–gel hydrolysis of zirconium n-propoxide and precipitation from zirconium oxychloride are distinct recipes. Each has oven (110 °C, 12 h) and Rotavapor vacuum (70 °C, 50 mbar, duration unreported) drying branches, followed by 400, 500, 600 or 700 °C calcination for 4 h in static air. The four uncalcined states remain separate supporting specimens.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Sections 2.1–2.3 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Sol–gel feed ambiguity is retained
intuition.text: The paper describes purchased 70 wt% zirconium propoxide solution, dilution to 30 wt%, a 0.025 M precursor and a typical charge of 17.7 g Zr-P plus 41.3 g n-propanol. Whether the stated precursor mass denotes stock solution or neat-equivalent reagent is unresolved. No molar charge or corrected concentration is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.2

intuition.title: Phase fractions and domain sizes are separate
intuition.text: Table 1 reports XRD peak-area tetragonal/monoclinic fractions; blank cells and the printed dash do not become inferred zeros. Table 2 gives phase/reflection-specific Scherrer crystallite sizes and lattice strains, not SEM particle diameters. Its strain unit or scale is unspecified. At 700 °C, SG-O is 23 nm in Table 2 but 20 nm in the prose; both are retained with the explicit table used in structured measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3,5–6, Tables 1–2 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Stabilization is an interpretation
intuition.text: The authors relate retention of tetragonal zirconia to small crystallites, hydroxyl groups and lattice strain, with greater thermal stability for sol–gel material. Vacuum drying initially produces larger domains. These explanations and the cited critical-size literature are not additional measured thresholds or current sample recipes. Exact residual tetragonal fractions at high temperature are retained instead of treating summarized complete transformation as zero.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4,6–7, Structural discussion and conclusions

intuition.title: Before-calcination morphology has its own scope
intuition.text: Figure 6 shows spherical sol–gel particles after either drying route. Precipitation gives predominantly cubic/rectangular particles of varying sizes after oven drying, with some spherical particles after vacuum drying. These images are before calcination; no numerical SEM particle mean or automatic post-calcination shape is assigned.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 6–7, Figure 6 and Section 3.4

intuition.title: Textural and thermal measurements
intuition.text: Table 3 reports only before-calcination and 400 °C textural values. Surface areas and pore volumes decrease while average pore diameters increase. Figure 5 shows before-calcination N2 isotherms, interpreted as combined H2/H3 hysteresis with ink-bottle and slit pores. TG/DTG weight loss of 22–33% and mechanisms remain study-level context without exact batch-specific values.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–7, Thermal discussion, Figure 5, Table 3 and Sections 3.2–3.3

intuition.title: Precursor and drying branches
intuition.text: Sol–gel hydrolysis of zirconium n-propoxide and precipitation from zirconium oxychloride are distinct recipes. Each has oven (110 °C, 12 h) and Rotavapor vacuum (70 °C, 50 mbar, duration unreported) drying branches, followed by 400, 500, 600 or 700 °C calcination for 4 h in static air. The four uncalcined states remain separate supporting specimens.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Sections 2.1–2.3 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Sol–gel feed ambiguity is retained
intuition.text: The paper describes purchased 70 wt% zirconium propoxide solution, dilution to 30 wt%, a 0.025 M precursor and a typical charge of 17.7 g Zr-P plus 41.3 g n-propanol. Whether the stated precursor mass denotes stock solution or neat-equivalent reagent is unresolved. No molar charge or corrected concentration is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.2

intuition.title: Phase fractions and domain sizes are separate
intuition.text: Table 1 reports XRD peak-area tetragonal/monoclinic fractions; blank cells and the printed dash do not become inferred zeros. Table 2 gives phase/reflection-specific Scherrer crystallite sizes and lattice strains, not SEM particle diameters. Its strain unit or scale is unspecified. At 700 °C, SG-O is 23 nm in Table 2 but 20 nm in the prose; both are retained with the explicit table used in structured measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3,5–6, Tables 1–2 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Stabilization is an interpretation
intuition.text: The authors relate retention of tetragonal zirconia to small crystallites, hydroxyl groups and lattice strain, with greater thermal stability for sol–gel material. Vacuum drying initially produces larger domains. These explanations and the cited critical-size literature are not additional measured thresholds or current sample recipes. Exact residual tetragonal fractions at high temperature are retained instead of treating summarized complete transformation as zero.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4,6–7, Structural discussion and conclusions

intuition.title: Before-calcination morphology has its own scope
intuition.text: Figure 6 shows spherical sol–gel particles after either drying route. Precipitation gives predominantly cubic/rectangular particles of varying sizes after oven drying, with some spherical particles after vacuum drying. These images are before calcination; no numerical SEM particle mean or automatic post-calcination shape is assigned.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 6–7, Figure 6 and Section 3.4

intuition.title: Textural and thermal measurements
intuition.text: Table 3 reports only before-calcination and 400 °C textural values. Surface areas and pore volumes decrease while average pore diameters increase. Figure 5 shows before-calcination N2 isotherms, interpreted as combined H2/H3 hysteresis with ink-bottle and slit pores. TG/DTG weight loss of 22–33% and mechanisms remain study-level context without exact batch-specific values.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–7, Thermal discussion, Figure 5, Table 3 and Sections 3.2–3.3

intuition.title: Stabilization is an interpretation

intuition.title: Fresh precursor rather than an aged-sol reconstruction
intuition.text: OH-form anion resin is added gradually to0.01M cerium(III)nitrate until pH10.0, then removed by filtration. Fresh sol is immediately treated in half-filled100mLPTFE autoclaves. Earlier sols aged several days and their6–8nm outcome belong to cited study20, not this paper’s nine conditions.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Experimental and fresh/aged comparison

intuition.title: Nine measured temperature/time conditions
intuition.text: The table resolves130/150/170°C at30 or180min, and190°C at30/120/180min. TEM means range5.4–6.0nm with no material temperature/time dependence claimed by the authors. Table bandgaps have reported±0.03eV. Physical batches and aliquot overlap are unspecified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Table and Results

intuition.title: Primary particles and aggregates are distinct
intuition.text: Mostly hexagonal particle outlines and occasional chain aggregates are described for cubic CeO2. Figure1 images three named conditions, Figure2 labels eight conditions, and Figure3 DLS curves label four; absent labels are not filled in. DLS sizes are not digitized from curves. Oriented attachment is the authors’ interpretation.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, TEM/DLS discussion and Figures1–3

intuition.title: Optical size is not the TEM mean
intuition.text: The source uses a cited semiempirical relation to infer a study-level characteristic size of about3.6–3.8nm from bandgap. This remains separate from the table TEM values and is not assigned as a new individual specimen measurement. Coarse CeO2 bandgap about3.2eV is comparison context.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Bandgap discussion, relation from reference26

intuition.title: Citrate and ATP procedures have different scope
intuition.text: Citrate adsorption uses0.1M sodium citrate at0.2–2.0mol/molceria and is most efficient atpH2–5. Filter and wash the sediment, then redisperse to aboutpH9 with NH4OH or NaOH; the NH4OH branch boils off excess ammonia. ATP solution is1% with2mol/LNaOH, amount unspecified. The namedAn-190-30-ATP sample has3.74eV; no new numeric TEM size is supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2,5, Stabilization procedures and named ATP outcome

intuition.title: Model and biomedical interpretation remain qualified
intuition.text: Figure4 is a steric model with two ATP molecules on a(CeO2)70cluster, not a measured particle structure or coordinates. Entire-pH-range ATP stability is qualitative and low-temperature storage is required without a numerical temperature. Sterilization feasibility and mitochondrial affinity are proposed applications, not new measured clinical or cell outcomes.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–5, Figure4 and biomedical discussion

intuition.title: Citrate and ATP procedures have different scope
intuition.text: Citrate adsorption uses0.1M sodium citrate at0.2–2.0mol/molceria and is most efficient atpH2–5. Filter and wash the sediment, then redisperse to aboutpH9 with NH4OH or NaOH; the NH4OH branch boils off excess ammonia. ATP solution is1% with2mol/LNaOH, amount unspecified. The namedAn-190-30-ATP sample has3.74eV; no new numeric TEM size is supplied.

intuition.title: Model and biomedical interpretation remain qualified
intuition.text: Figure4 is a steric model with two ATP molecules on a(CeO2)70cluster, not a measured particle structure or coordinates. Sterilization feasibility and mitochondrial affinity are proposed applications, not new measured clinical or cell outcomes.

intuition.title: Thiolactic acid links PbS to the nanotube host
intuition.text: The authors use thiolactic acid to attach PbS to TiO2 nanotubes. The both-surface route uses 0.6 M TLA; outer-surface DDAB blocking followed by 0.3 M TLA directs deposition into the pores. The lower TLA concentration was chosen in an effort to match size; a separate numerical inside-only size is not established.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Deposition and Figure 1 discussion

intuition.title: Charge and dye identity govern the assay comparison
intuition.text: Around pH 6 the TNT surfaces favor cationic-dye adsorption. Figures 2–4 report the order PbS/TNTs > TNTs > PbS/TNTs (in) > P25 for methylene blue, methylene green and rhodamine B. For indigo carmine and rose bengal, Figures 5–6 instead show P25 > PbS/TNTs > PbS/TNTs (in) > TNTs. These are source activity comparisons, not additional syntheses.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Photocatalytic Activity and Figures 2–6

intuition.title: Inside-only deposition may restrict access
intuition.text: The authors propose that PbS in the pores reduces accessible TNT surface and that remaining blocking reagent may also reduce activity. These are proposed explanations; remaining DDAB and pore-blocking fractions are not measured quantitatively in the main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Inside-only catalyst interpretation

intuition.title: Filtered-light response supports a qualified transfer mechanism
intuition.text: With a Ray-sorb reactor filtering light below 600 nm, methylene-blue degradation is observed with PbS/TNTs whereas TNTs alone do not catalyze bleaching. Close contact through the linker is proposed to permit electron transfer. Literature energy levels and a size-dependent transfer limit are contextual estimates, not measured band alignment for a identified batch.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–5, Effect of PbS QDs and Figure 7

intuition.title: Recycling separates activity from catalyst recovery
intuition.text: Figure 8 compares three methylene-blue runs at a 30 min readout. The authors discuss incomplete particle recovery, possible corrosion and dye adsorption as explanations for changes. FTIR is said to show no PbS oxidation, but the spectrum is not shown. No exact bar values are digitized.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 5, Recyclability and Figure 8

intuition.title: Thiolactic acid links PbS to the nanotube host
intuition.text: The authors use thiolactic acid to attach PbS to TiO2 nanotubes. The both-surface route uses 0.6 M TLA; outer-surface DDAB blocking followed by 0.3 M TLA directs deposition into the pores. The lower TLA concentration was chosen in an effort to match size; a separate numerical inside-only size is not established.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Deposition and Figure 1 discussion

intuition.title: Charge and dye identity govern the assay comparison
intuition.text: Around pH 6 the TNT surfaces favor cationic-dye adsorption. Figures 2–4 report the order PbS/TNTs > TNTs > PbS/TNTs (in) > P25 for methylene blue, methylene green and rhodamine B. For indigo carmine and rose bengal, Figures 5–6 instead show P25 > PbS/TNTs > PbS/TNTs (in) > TNTs. These are source activity comparisons, not additional syntheses.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Photocatalytic Activity and Figures 2–6

intuition.title: Inside-only deposition may restrict access
intuition.text: The authors propose that PbS in the pores reduces accessible TNT surface and that remaining blocking reagent may also reduce activity. These are proposed explanations; remaining DDAB and pore-blocking fractions are not measured quantitatively in the main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Inside-only catalyst interpretation

intuition.title: Filtered-light response supports a qualified transfer mechanism
intuition.text: With a Ray-sorb reactor filtering light below 600 nm, methylene-blue degradation is observed with PbS/TNTs whereas TNTs alone do not catalyze bleaching. Close contact through the linker is proposed to permit electron transfer. Literature energy levels and a size-dependent transfer limit are contextual estimates, not measured band alignment for a identified batch.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–5, Effect of PbS QDs and Figure 7

intuition.title: Recycling separates activity from catalyst recovery
intuition.text: Figure 8 compares three methylene-blue runs at a 30 min readout. The authors discuss incomplete particle recovery, possible corrosion and dye adsorption as explanations for changes. FTIR is said to show no PbS oxidation, but the spectrum is not shown. No exact bar values are digitized.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 5, Recyclability and Figure 8

intuition.title: Core growth and assembly are different procedures
intuition.text: The two metal preparations differ in solvent and ligand timing: Au uses toluene and dodecanethiol after reduction, while Ag uses chloroform and dodecanethiol before borohydride. Film conditions use preformed particles; they do not establish new independent core-synthesis batches.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.1–2, Experimental

intuition.title: Superlattice packing is not atomic crystal phase
intuition.text: The detailed results identify fcc packing of nanocrystals and a (111)s plane parallel to the substrate. The summary instead says normal; the discrepancy is retained. Atomic Au/Ag phase, lattice parameters and coordinates are not supplied by these SEM observations.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.2,5, orientation and Summary

intuition.title: Solvent and sonication select different assemblies
intuition.text: Au hexane gives rough mounds, whereas chloroform gives relatively smooth films with triangular step-growth features. The 9:1 hexane/ethanol mixture gives dendritic, nonordered deposits without sonication and faceted superlattice crystallites with sonication during casting. Sonication of good-solvent hexane/toluene dispersions did not produce homogeneous superlattice nucleation.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.2–3, Figures2–4

intuition.title: Temperature affects film morphology, not a reported new core size
intuition.text: Au films from toluene have mounds at room temperature and become flatter but locally disordered at 40°C. Many more defects than in room-temperature chloroform films remain. No new particle size is assigned to this temperature comparison.
intuition.source_locator: Main p.4, Figure5

intuition.title: Surface diffusion interpretation is model-scoped
intuition.text: The authors discuss bulk diffusion, adsorption, surface diffusion and incorporation or desorption. More attractive interactions and larger supersaturation favor short surface diffusion and radial mound growth; lower supersaturation and longer diffusion favor step growth. The roughly ten-diameter or60nm diffusion scale is an estimate, not measured core or mound size.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.4–5, Discussion

intuition.title: SI optical results do not create structural specimens
intuition.text: The SI follows separately prepared Au dispersions in two solvents using absorbance. Final concentrations, elapsed times and fractional losses stay with their optical experiments. Their particle size and exact link to a main-film specimen are unknown. Small short-time changes are interpreted by the authors as insufficient to explain the main solvent-dependent film differences.
intuition.source_locator: SI pp.3–5, FigureS2
