intuition.title: Core growth and assembly are different procedures
intuition.text: The two metal preparations differ in solvent and ligand timing: Au uses toluene and dodecanethiol after reduction, while Ag uses chloroform and dodecanethiol before borohydride. Film conditions use preformed particles; they do not establish new independent core-synthesis batches.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.1–2, Experimental

intuition.title: Superlattice packing is not atomic crystal phase
intuition.text: The detailed results identify fcc packing of nanocrystals and a (111)s plane parallel to the substrate. The summary instead says normal; the discrepancy is retained. Atomic Au/Ag phase, lattice parameters and coordinates are not supplied by these SEM observations.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.2,5, orientation and Summary

intuition.title: Solvent and sonication select different assemblies
intuition.text: Au hexane gives rough mounds, whereas chloroform gives relatively smooth films with triangular step-growth features. The 9:1 hexane/ethanol mixture gives dendritic, nonordered deposits without sonication and faceted superlattice crystallites with sonication during casting. Sonication of good-solvent hexane/toluene dispersions did not produce homogeneous superlattice nucleation.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.2–3, Figures2–4

intuition.title: Temperature affects film morphology, not a reported new core size
intuition.text: Au films from toluene have mounds at room temperature and become flatter but locally disordered at 40°C. Many more defects than in room-temperature chloroform films remain. No new particle size is assigned to this temperature comparison.
intuition.source_locator: Main p.4, Figure5

intuition.title: Surface diffusion interpretation is model-scoped
intuition.text: The authors discuss bulk diffusion, adsorption, surface diffusion and incorporation or desorption. More attractive interactions and larger supersaturation favor short surface diffusion and radial mound growth; lower supersaturation and longer diffusion favor step growth. The roughly ten-diameter or60nm diffusion scale is an estimate, not measured core or mound size.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.4–5, Discussion

intuition.title: SI optical results do not create structural specimens
intuition.text: The SI follows separately prepared Au dispersions in two solvents using absorbance. Final concentrations, elapsed times and fractional losses stay with their optical experiments. Their particle size and exact link to a main-film specimen are unknown. Small short-time changes are interpreted by the authors as insufficient to explain the main solvent-dependent film differences.
intuition.source_locator: SI pp.3–5, FigureS2

intuition.title: Core growth and assembly are different procedures

intuition.source_locator: Main pp.1–2, Experimental

intuition.title: Superlattice packing is not atomic crystal phase
intuition.text: The detailed results identify fcc packing of nanocrystals and a (111)s plane parallel to the substrate. The summary instead says normal; the discrepancy is retained. Atomic Au/Ag phase, lattice parameters and coordinates are not supplied by these SEM observations.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.2,5, orientation and Summary

intuition.title: Solvent and sonication select different assemblies
intuition.text: Au hexane gives rough mounds, whereas chloroform gives relatively smooth films with triangular step-growth features. The 9:1 hexane/ethanol mixture gives dendritic, nonordered deposits without sonication and faceted superlattice crystallites with sonication during casting. Sonication of good-solvent hexane/toluene dispersions did not produce homogeneous superlattice nucleation.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.2–3, Figures2–4

intuition.title: Temperature affects film morphology, not a reported new core size
intuition.text: Au films from toluene have mounds at room temperature and become flatter but locally disordered at 40°C. Many more defects than in room-temperature chloroform films remain. No new particle size is assigned to this temperature comparison.
intuition.source_locator: Main p.4, Figure5

intuition.title: Surface diffusion interpretation is model-scoped
intuition.text: The authors discuss bulk diffusion, adsorption, surface diffusion and incorporation or desorption. More attractive interactions and larger supersaturation favor short surface diffusion and radial mound growth; lower supersaturation and longer diffusion favor step growth. The roughly ten-diameter or60nm diffusion scale is an estimate, not measured core or mound size.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.4–5, Discussion

intuition.title: SI optical results do not create structural specimens
intuition.text: The SI follows separately prepared Au dispersions in two solvents using absorbance. Final concentrations, elapsed times and fractional losses stay with their optical experiments. Their particle size and exact link to a main-film specimen are unknown. Small short-time changes are interpreted by the authors as insufficient to explain the main solvent-dependent film differences.

intuition.title: Core growth and assembly are different procedures
intuition.text: The two metal preparations differ in solvent and ligand timing: Au uses toluene and dodecanethiol after reduction, while Ag uses chloroform and dodecanethiol before borohydride. Film conditions use preformed particles; they do not establish new independent core-synthesis batches.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.1–2, Experimental

intuition.title: Superlattice packing is not atomic crystal phase
intuition.text: The detailed results identify fcc packing of nanocrystals and a (111)s plane parallel to the substrate. The summary instead says normal; the discrepancy is retained. Atomic Au/Ag phase, lattice parameters and coordinates are not supplied by these SEM observations.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.2,5, orientation and Summary

intuition.title: Solvent and sonication select different assemblies
intuition.text: Au hexane gives rough mounds, whereas chloroform gives relatively smooth films with triangular step-growth features. The 9:1 hexane/ethanol mixture gives dendritic, nonordered deposits without sonication and faceted superlattice crystallites with sonication during casting. Sonication of good-solvent hexane/toluene dispersions did not produce homogeneous superlattice nucleation.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.2–3, Figures2–4

intuition.title: Temperature affects film morphology, not a reported new core size
intuition.text: Au films from toluene have mounds at room temperature and become flatter but locally disordered at 40°C. Many more defects than in room-temperature chloroform films remain. No new particle size is assigned to this temperature comparison.
intuition.source_locator: Main p.4, Figure5

intuition.title: Surface diffusion interpretation is model-scoped
intuition.text: The authors discuss bulk diffusion, adsorption, surface diffusion and incorporation or desorption. More attractive interactions and larger supersaturation favor short surface diffusion and radial mound growth; lower supersaturation and longer diffusion favor step growth. The roughly ten-diameter or60nm diffusion scale is an estimate, not measured core or mound size.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.4–5, Discussion

intuition.title: SI optical results do not create structural specimens
intuition.text: The SI follows separately prepared Au dispersions in two solvents using absorbance. Final concentrations, elapsed times and fractional losses stay with their optical experiments. Their particle size and exact link to a main-film specimen are unknown. Small short-time changes are interpreted by the authors as insufficient to explain the main solvent-dependent film differences.
intuition.source_locator: SI pp.3–5, FigureS2

intuition.title: Three related cores share a two-stage shelling route
intuition.text: CIS, CIGS and ZCIS differ in explicitly stated core-cation feed. OTT supplies sulfur and passivates the surface; two separately prepared zinc feeds grow ZnS shells for one hour each at240°C. Feed ratios do not measure final core stoichiometry.
intuition.source_locator: Main p.6, Experimental

intuition.title: Only one oxide composition has absolute salt charges
intuition.text: The Zn0.95Mg0.05O example uses2.85mmol Zn acetate dihydrate and0.15mmol Mg acetate tetrahydrate in30mL DMSO. The x=0 and0.1 variants adjust molar proportions with other parameters fixed. Their salt charges and the concentration/form of5mL TMAH remain unknown.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.6–7, Experimental

intuition.title: Size evidence remains specimen-specific
intuition.text: TEM mean3.2nm is assigned to CIGS/ZnS only. ZnO andZn0.9Mg0.1O have4.2nm and3.1nm means respectively; the x=0.05 size is not given. Similar-size wording and additional ZCIS images do not establish missing numeric means.
intuition.source_locator: Main p.3, Figures1–2; SI FiguresS1–S2

intuition.title: Dispersion and film energy levels are different measurements
intuition.text: Optical bandgaps of ZnMgO dispersions are3.73,3.89,4.07eV, while solid-film TableS1 gives3.66,3.82,3.93eV. UPS tabulates positive binding energies below vacuum; the QD PESA diagram uses signed negative vacuum-referenced energies. These conventions and specimen states are preserved.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.3–4; SI TableS1 and FigureS3

intuition.title: Nine devices do not represent nine additional nanoparticle batches
intuition.text: Three QD EMLs combine with three ZnMgO ETLs. The common fabrication method and exact maxima remain source-specific. Figure4b cross-section depicts only CIS/ZnS withZn0.95Mg0.05O; no other device borrows that image as its measured specimen.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.4–7, Figures4–7

intuition.title: Efficiency interpretation is qualified
intuition.text: Raising the oxide conduction band with Mg is proposed to improve electron injection. CIS device efficiency peaks atx=0.05, while CIGS and ZCIS efficiency increases throughx=0.1. Excess electron injection is a proposed explanation for the CIS efficiency decrease, not an independently established causal measurement.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.5–6, Discussion

intuition.title: Three related cores share a two-stage shelling route
intuition.text: CIS, CIGS and ZCIS differ in explicitly stated core-cation feed. OTT supplies sulfur and passivates the surface; two separately prepared zinc feeds grow ZnS shells for one hour each at240°C. Feed ratios do not measure final core stoichiometry.
intuition.source_locator: Main p.6, Experimental

intuition.title: Only one oxide composition has absolute salt charges
intuition.text: The Zn0.95Mg0.05O example uses2.85mmol Zn acetate dihydrate and0.15mmol Mg acetate tetrahydrate in30mL DMSO. The x=0 and0.1 variants adjust molar proportions with other parameters fixed. Their salt charges and the concentration/form of5mL TMAH remain unknown.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.6–7, Experimental

intuition.title: Size evidence remains specimen-specific
intuition.text: TEM mean3.2nm is assigned to CIGS/ZnS only. ZnO andZn0.9Mg0.1O have4.2nm and3.1nm means respectively; the x=0.05 size is not given. Similar-size wording and additional ZCIS images do not establish missing numeric means.
intuition.source_locator: Main p.3, Figures1–2; SI FiguresS1–S2

intuition.title: Dispersion and film energy levels are different measurements
intuition.text: Optical bandgaps of ZnMgO dispersions are3.73,3.89,4.07eV, while solid-film TableS1 gives3.66,3.82,3.93eV. UPS tabulates positive binding energies below vacuum; the QD PESA diagram uses signed negative vacuum-referenced energies. These conventions and specimen states are preserved.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.3–4; SI TableS1 and FigureS3

intuition.title: Nine devices do not represent nine additional nanoparticle batches
intuition.text: Three QD EMLs combine with three ZnMgO ETLs. The common fabrication method and exact maxima remain source-specific. Figure4b cross-section depicts only CIS/ZnS withZn0.95Mg0.05O; no other device borrows that image as its measured specimen.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.4–7, Figures4–7

intuition.title: Efficiency interpretation is qualified
intuition.text: Raising the oxide conduction band with Mg is proposed to improve electron injection. CIS device efficiency peaks atx=0.05, while CIGS and ZCIS efficiency increases throughx=0.1. Excess electron injection is a proposed explanation for the CIS efficiency decrease, not an independently established causal measurement.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.5–6, Discussion

intuition.title: Dispersion and film energy levels are different measurements
intuition.text: Optical bandgaps of ZnMgO dispersions are3.73,3.89,4.07eV, while solid-film TableS1 gives3.66,3.82,3.93eV. UPS tabulates positive binding energies below vacuum; the QD PESA diagram uses signed negative vacuum-referenced energies. These conventions and specimen states are preserved.

intuition.title: Efficiency interpretation is qualified

intuition.title: Only one oxide composition has absolute salt charges

intuition.title: Size evidence remains specimen-specific

intuition.title: Dispersion and film energy levels are different measurements
intuition.text: Optical bandgaps of ZnMgO dispersions are3.73,3.89,4.07eV, while solid-film TableS1 gives3.66,3.82,3.93eV. UPS tabulates positive binding energies below vacuum; the QD PESA diagram uses signed negative vacuum-referenced energies. These conventions and specimen states are preserved.

intuition.title: Nine devices do not represent nine additional nanoparticle batches
intuition.text: Three QD EMLs combine with three ZnMgO ETLs. The common fabrication method and exact maxima remain source-specific. Figure4b cross-section depicts only CIS/ZnS withZn0.95Mg0.05O; no other device borrows that image as its measured specimen.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp.4–7, Figures4–7

intuition.title: Efficiency interpretation is qualified
intuition.text: Raising the oxide conduction band with Mg is proposed to improve electron injection. CIS device efficiency peaks atx=0.05, while CIGS and ZCIS efficiency increases throughx=0.1. Excess electron injection is a proposed explanation for the CIS efficiency decrease, not an independently established causal measurement.

intuition.title: Study context: Source-proposed LSS mechanism
intuition.text: The authors describe ion exchange from aqueous metal ions into solid metal linoleate, interfacial reaction, hydrophobic fatty-acid-associated surfaces and spontaneous separation. Figure 3 is their mechanistic scheme, not measured molecular or particle coordinates. Its reduction-by-ethanol step applies to noble metals; other material families use different interfacial chemistry.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, LSS mechanism and Figure 3

intuition.title: Study context: Noble-metal quantities have bounded scope
intuition.text: The typical noble-metal recipe specifies 20 mL aqueous salt solution with an example 0.5 g salt charge, 1.6 g sodium linoleate, 10 mL ethanol and 2 mL linoleic acid in a 40 mL autoclave, sealed for 10 h. AgNO3 and HAuCl4 are named; other soluble chlorides are unspecified. No hydration state or exact salt identity is added. Other fatty acids and corresponding salts are stated alternatives, not extra quantified runs.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, Typical synthesis

intuition.title: Study context: Ranges are not a series of invented experiments
intuition.text: Source family temperatures are Ag 80–200 °C; Ru/Rh/Ir 20–200 °C; Au/Pd/Pt 20–100 °C. Ag/Au diameter can vary about 4–15 nm, and Ru/Rh/Ir/Pd/Pt are about 3 nm or less. Specific Figure 1 captions retain their own means, uncertainty and temperature. SI tuning series were not reviewed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Noble metals and Figure 1a

intuition.title: Study context: Different non-noble reactions retain missing inputs
intuition.text: The source names sulfide from Na2S or (NH4)2S, selenide from SeO3(2−) reduced by N2H4, and fluoride from NaF or NH4F. Figure captions supply selected ratios and temperatures. Unassigned alternatives remain unresolved and the noble-metal 10 h/liquid charges are not transferred. Barium titanate alone has the stated 7 g NaOH, 0.5 g Ba(NO3)2 and equal TiCl3 moles; TiO2 has 1 mL 30% TiCl3 for a 40 mL vessel.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Material families and Figure 1 caption

intuition.title: Study context: Hierarchical sizes and source discrepancies
intuition.text: YF3 rice-like assemblies are approximately 100 nm across and 500 nm long, composed of approximately 5 nm nanocrystals. The NaYF4/LaF3/YbF3 family range 4–12 nm and Ln(OH)3 nanorod diameters 3–15 nm vary with temperature and do not become extra specimen means. CoFe2O4 caption 11.5±0.6 nm is retained separately from the prose approximation of about 10 nm.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figure 1 caption and morphology discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Characterization and processing context
intuition.text: TEM-grid assembly occurs after solvent evaporation; original image scales are not size averages. Figure 2 CdS is not the Figure 1 CdSe specimen. Cyclohexane/chloroform dispersions are usually stable for months; Figure 4 calls 2% a typical concentration without specifying percentage basis. Drop/dip coating, ethanol reprecipitation and external-field separation are qualitative downstream possibilities, without exact dose/schedule or new synthesis measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, TEM arrays, Figures 2/4 and processing discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Source-proposed LSS mechanism
intuition.text: The authors describe ion exchange from aqueous metal ions into solid metal linoleate, interfacial reaction, hydrophobic fatty-acid-associated surfaces and spontaneous separation. Figure 3 is their mechanistic scheme, not measured molecular or particle coordinates. Its reduction-by-ethanol step applies to noble metals; other material families use different interfacial chemistry.

intuition.title: Study context: Noble-metal quantities have bounded scope
intuition.text: The typical noble-metal recipe specifies 20 mL aqueous salt solution with an example 0.5 g salt charge, 1.6 g sodium linoleate, 10 mL ethanol and 2 mL linoleic acid in a 40 mL autoclave, sealed for 10 h. AgNO3 and HAuCl4 are named; other soluble chlorides are unspecified. No hydration state or exact salt identity is added. Other fatty acids and corresponding salts are stated alternatives, not extra quantified runs.

intuition.title: Study context: Source-proposed LSS mechanism
intuition.text: The authors describe ion exchange from aqueous metal ions into solid metal linoleate, interfacial reaction, hydrophobic fatty-acid-associated surfaces and spontaneous separation. Figure 3 is their mechanistic scheme, not measured molecular or particle coordinates. Its reduction-by-ethanol step applies to noble metals; other material families use different interfacial chemistry.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, LSS mechanism and Figure 3

intuition.title: Study context: Noble-metal quantities have bounded scope
intuition.text: The typical noble-metal recipe specifies 20 mL aqueous salt solution with an example 0.5 g salt charge, 1.6 g sodium linoleate, 10 mL ethanol and 2 mL linoleic acid in a 40 mL autoclave, sealed for 10 h. AgNO3 and HAuCl4 are named; other soluble chlorides are unspecified. No hydration state or exact salt identity is added. Other fatty acids and corresponding salts are stated alternatives, not extra quantified runs.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, Typical synthesis

intuition.title: Study context: Ranges are not a series of invented experiments
intuition.text: Source family temperatures are Ag 80–200 °C; Ru/Rh/Ir 20–200 °C; Au/Pd/Pt 20–100 °C. Ag/Au diameter can vary about 4–15 nm, and Ru/Rh/Ir/Pd/Pt are about 3 nm or less. Specific Figure 1 captions retain their own means, uncertainty and temperature. SI tuning series were not reviewed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Noble metals and Figure 1a

intuition.title: Study context: Different non-noble reactions retain missing inputs
intuition.text: The source names sulfide from Na2S or (NH4)2S, selenide from SeO3(2−) reduced by N2H4, and fluoride from NaF or NH4F. Figure captions supply selected ratios and temperatures. Unassigned alternatives remain unresolved and the noble-metal 10 h/liquid charges are not transferred. Barium titanate alone has the stated 7 g NaOH, 0.5 g Ba(NO3)2 and equal TiCl3 moles; TiO2 has 1 mL 30% TiCl3 for a 40 mL vessel.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Material families and Figure 1 caption

intuition.title: Study context: Hierarchical sizes and source discrepancies
intuition.text: YF3 rice-like assemblies are approximately 100 nm across and 500 nm long, composed of approximately 5 nm nanocrystals. The NaYF4/LaF3/YbF3 family range 4–12 nm and Ln(OH)3 nanorod diameters 3–15 nm vary with temperature and do not become extra specimen means. CoFe2O4 caption 11.5±0.6 nm is retained separately from the prose approximation of about 10 nm.

intuition.title: Study context: Characterization and processing context

Drop/dip coating, ethanol reprecipitation and external-field separation are qualitative downstream possibilities, without exact dose/schedule or new synthesis measurements.

intuition.title: Study context: Source-proposed LSS mechanism
intuition.text: The authors describe ion exchange from aqueous metal ions into solid metal linoleate, interfacial reaction, hydrophobic fatty-acid-associated surfaces and spontaneous separation. Figure 3 is their mechanistic scheme, not measured molecular or particle coordinates. Its reduction-by-ethanol step applies to noble metals; other material families use different interfacial chemistry.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, LSS mechanism and Figure 3

intuition.title: Study context: Noble-metal quantities have bounded scope
intuition.text: The typical noble-metal recipe specifies 20 mL aqueous salt solution with an example 0.5 g salt charge, 1.6 g sodium linoleate, 10 mL ethanol and 2 mL linoleic acid in a 40 mL autoclave, sealed for 10 h. AgNO3 and HAuCl4 are named; other soluble chlorides are unspecified. No hydration state or exact salt identity is added. Other fatty acids and corresponding salts are stated alternatives, not extra quantified runs.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, Typical synthesis

intuition.title: Study context: Ranges are not a series of invented experiments
intuition.text: Source family temperatures are Ag 80–200 °C; Ru/Rh/Ir 20–200 °C; Au/Pd/Pt 20–100 °C. Ag/Au diameter can vary about 4–15 nm, and Ru/Rh/Ir/Pd/Pt are about 3 nm or less. Specific Figure 1 captions retain their own means, uncertainty and temperature. SI tuning series were not reviewed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Noble metals and Figure 1a

intuition.title: Study context: Different non-noble reactions retain missing inputs
intuition.text: The source names sulfide from Na2S or (NH4)2S, selenide from SeO3(2−) reduced by N2H4, and fluoride from NaF or NH4F. Figure captions supply selected ratios and temperatures. Unassigned alternatives remain unresolved and the noble-metal 10 h/liquid charges are not transferred. Barium titanate alone has the stated 7 g NaOH, 0.5 g Ba(NO3)2 and equal TiCl3 moles; TiO2 has 1 mL 30% TiCl3 for a 40 mL vessel.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Material families and Figure 1 caption

intuition.title: Study context: Hierarchical sizes and source discrepancies
intuition.text: YF3 rice-like assemblies are approximately 100 nm across and 500 nm long, composed of approximately 5 nm nanocrystals. The NaYF4/LaF3/YbF3 family range 4–12 nm and Ln(OH)3 nanorod diameters 3–15 nm vary with temperature and do not become extra specimen means. CoFe2O4 caption 11.5±0.6 nm is retained separately from the prose approximation of about 10 nm.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figure 1 caption and morphology discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Characterization and processing context
intuition.text: TEM-grid assembly occurs after solvent evaporation; original image scales are not size averages. Figure 2 CdS is not the Figure 1 CdSe specimen. Cyclohexane/chloroform dispersions are usually stable for months; Figure 4 calls 2% a typical concentration without specifying percentage basis. Drop/dip coating, ethanol reprecipitation and external-field separation are qualitative downstream possibilities, without exact dose/schedule or new synthesis measurements.

intuition.title: Study context: Noble-metal quantities have bounded scope
intuition.text: The typical noble-metal recipe specifies 20 mL aqueous salt solution with an example 0.5 g salt charge, 1.6 g sodium linoleate, 10 mL ethanol and 2 mL linoleic acid in a 40 mL autoclave, sealed for 10 h. AgNO3 and HAuCl4 are named; other soluble chlorides are unspecified. No hydration state or exact salt identity is added. Other fatty acids and corresponding salts are stated alternatives, not extra quantified runs.

intuition.title: Study context: Ranges are not a series of invented experiments

intuition.title: Study context: Different non-noble reactions retain missing inputs

intuition.title: Study context: Source-proposed LSS mechanism
intuition.text: The authors describe ion exchange from aqueous metal ions into solid metal linoleate, interfacial reaction, hydrophobic fatty-acid-associated surfaces and spontaneous separation. Figure 3 is their mechanistic scheme, not measured molecular or particle coordinates. Its reduction-by-ethanol step applies to noble metals; other material families use different interfacial chemistry.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, LSS mechanism and Figure 3

intuition.title: Study context: Noble-metal quantities have bounded scope
intuition.text: The typical noble-metal recipe specifies 20 mL aqueous salt solution with an example 0.5 g salt charge, 1.6 g sodium linoleate, 10 mL ethanol and 2 mL linoleic acid in a 40 mL autoclave, sealed for 10 h. AgNO3 and HAuCl4 are named; other soluble chlorides are unspecified. No hydration state or exact salt identity is added. Other fatty acids and corresponding salts are stated alternatives, not extra quantified runs.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, Typical synthesis

intuition.title: Study context: Ranges are not a series of invented experiments
intuition.text: Source family temperatures are Ag 80–200 °C; Ru/Rh/Ir 20–200 °C; Au/Pd/Pt 20–100 °C. Ag/Au diameter can vary about 4–15 nm, and Ru/Rh/Ir/Pd/Pt are about 3 nm or less. Specific Figure 1 captions retain their own means, uncertainty and temperature. SI tuning series were not reviewed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Noble metals and Figure 1a

intuition.title: Study context: Different non-noble reactions retain missing inputs
intuition.text: The source names sulfide from Na2S or (NH4)2S, selenide from SeO3(2−) reduced by N2H4, and fluoride from NaF or NH4F. Figure captions supply selected ratios and temperatures. Unassigned alternatives remain unresolved and the noble-metal 10 h/liquid charges are not transferred. Barium titanate alone has the stated 7 g NaOH, 0.5 g Ba(NO3)2 and equal TiCl3 moles; TiO2 has 1 mL 30% TiCl3 for a 40 mL vessel.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Material families and Figure 1 caption

intuition.title: Study context: Hierarchical sizes and source discrepancies
intuition.text: YF3 rice-like assemblies are approximately 100 nm across and 500 nm long, composed of approximately 5 nm nanocrystals. The NaYF4/LaF3/YbF3 family range 4–12 nm and Ln(OH)3 nanorod diameters 3–15 nm vary with temperature and do not become extra specimen means. CoFe2O4 caption 11.5±0.6 nm is retained separately from the prose approximation of about 10 nm.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figure 1 caption and morphology discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Characterization and processing context
intuition.text: TEM-grid assembly occurs after solvent evaporation; original image scales are not size averages. Figure 2 CdS is not the Figure 1 CdSe specimen. Cyclohexane/chloroform dispersions are usually stable for months; Figure 4 calls 2% a typical concentration without specifying percentage basis. Drop/dip coating, ethanol reprecipitation and external-field separation are qualitative downstream possibilities, without exact dose/schedule or new synthesis measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, TEM arrays, Figures 2/4 and processing discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Source-proposed LSS mechanism
intuition.text: The authors describe ion exchange from aqueous metal ions into solid metal linoleate, interfacial reaction, hydrophobic fatty-acid-associated surfaces and spontaneous separation. Figure 3 is their mechanistic scheme, not measured molecular or particle coordinates. Its reduction-by-ethanol step applies to noble metals; other material families use different interfacial chemistry.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, LSS mechanism and Figure 3

intuition.title: Study context: Noble-metal quantities have bounded scope
intuition.text: The typical noble-metal recipe specifies 20 mL aqueous salt solution with an example 0.5 g salt charge, 1.6 g sodium linoleate, 10 mL ethanol and 2 mL linoleic acid in a 40 mL autoclave, sealed for 10 h. AgNO3 and HAuCl4 are named; other soluble chlorides are unspecified. No hydration state or exact salt identity is added. Other fatty acids and corresponding salts are stated alternatives, not extra quantified runs.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, Typical synthesis

intuition.title: Study context: Ranges are not a series of invented experiments
intuition.text: Source family temperatures are Ag 80–200 °C; Ru/Rh/Ir 20–200 °C; Au/Pd/Pt 20–100 °C. Ag/Au diameter can vary about 4–15 nm, and Ru/Rh/Ir/Pd/Pt are about 3 nm or less. Specific Figure 1 captions retain their own means, uncertainty and temperature. SI tuning series were not reviewed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Noble metals and Figure 1a

intuition.title: Study context: Different non-noble reactions retain missing inputs
intuition.text: The source names sulfide from Na2S or (NH4)2S, selenide from SeO3(2−) reduced by N2H4, and fluoride from NaF or NH4F. Figure captions supply selected ratios and temperatures. Unassigned alternatives remain unresolved and the noble-metal 10 h/liquid charges are not transferred. Barium titanate alone has the stated 7 g NaOH, 0.5 g Ba(NO3)2 and equal TiCl3 moles; TiO2 has 1 mL 30% TiCl3 for a 40 mL vessel.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Material families and Figure 1 caption

intuition.title: Study context: Hierarchical sizes and source discrepancies
intuition.text: YF3 rice-like assemblies are approximately 100 nm across and 500 nm long, composed of approximately 5 nm nanocrystals. The NaYF4/LaF3/YbF3 family range 4–12 nm and Ln(OH)3 nanorod diameters 3–15 nm vary with temperature and do not become extra specimen means. CoFe2O4 caption 11.5±0.6 nm is retained separately from the prose approximation of about 10 nm.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figure 1 caption and morphology discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Characterization and processing context
intuition.text: TEM-grid assembly occurs after solvent evaporation; original image scales are not size averages. Figure 2 CdS is not the Figure 1 CdSe specimen. Cyclohexane/chloroform dispersions are usually stable for months; Figure 4 calls 2% a typical concentration without specifying percentage basis. Drop/dip coating, ethanol reprecipitation and external-field separation are qualitative downstream possibilities, without exact dose/schedule or new synthesis measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, TEM arrays, Figures 2/4 and processing discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Two quantified material routes
intuition.text: AgCl, elemental Ga or In, and sulfur are treated with ethylenediamine in a 50 mL autoclave filled to 85%, within 180–230 °C for 10 h. The reported metal charges differ: Ga 0.648 g or In 1.068 g. The source does not assign the exact temperature of either Figure 1/2 sample.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, Typical procedure and Figure 1

intuition.title: Study context: Solvent coordination is a source interpretation
intuition.text: The authors propose that basic, bidentate ethylenediamine forms a relatively stable Ag+ complex, incorporates dissolved sulfur and permits a liquid–solution diffusion process as Ga melts. Pyridine yields incomplete reaction and lower purity under otherwise constant conditions. Benzene yields mostly unreacted AgCl and Ga and no AgGaS2 by XRD. These comparisons are AgGaS2-specific and are not assigned to AgInS2.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Solvent-role discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Separate crystallite and particle sizes
intuition.text: Scherrer estimates are 6 nm for AgGaS2 and 10 nm for AgInS2. TEM diameter ranges are 5–7 and 9–12 nm, respectively. Figure 2 caption links its specimens to Figure 1. Image scale bars are preserved but are not substituted for particle sizes.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, XRD/Scherrer and TEM discussion; Figures 1–2

intuition.title: Study context: Comparisons are not invented discrete trials
intuition.text: For AgGaS2, below 150 °C OR shorter than 5 h gives lower crystallinity; above 250 °C OR longer than 12 h gives larger particles and solvent-carbonization contamination. Exact tested values, paired time/temperature and numerical sizes are not given. The four inequality statements are separate supporting observations, not combined conditions.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Temperature and time comparisons

intuition.title: Study context: Analytical limits and future extensions
intuition.text: XPS detects no obvious chloride or elemental sulfur impurities at a stated 1 at% resolution limit; this is an analytical limit, not a measured impurity value. The Ag:Ga:S ratio 1:1.08:2.10 belongs only to AgGaS2. Proposed extension to AgMSe2 and CuMS2 (M=Ga, In) is an outlook, not an achieved additional synthesis. Background optical properties and high-temperature solid-state routes belong to cited literature.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, XPS, introduction and conclusion

intuition.title: Study context: Solvent coordination is a source interpretation
intuition.text: The authors propose that basic, bidentate ethylenediamine forms a relatively stable Ag+ complex, incorporates dissolved sulfur and permits a liquid–solution diffusion process as Ga melts. intuition.title: Study context: Solvent coordination is a source interpretation
intuition.text: The authors propose that basic, bidentate ethylenediamine forms a relatively stable Ag+ complex, incorporates dissolved sulfur and permits a liquid–solution diffusion process as Ga melts. These comparisons are AgGaS2-specific and are not assigned to AgInS2.

intuition.title: Study context: Analytical limits and future extensions

intuition.title: Distinct structural dimensions
intuition.text: The authors report approximately 7 ± 1 nm CdS particles, approximately 20 nm sharp-edged aggregates, approximately 8.2 nm Scherrer grains and approximately 150 nm film thickness. These describe different objects and are not interchangeable. The statistic represented by ±1 nm is not identified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Film preparation, Figure 1 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Crystallinity is qualified
intuition.text: SAED has diffuse rings, which the authors associate with significant amorphous and/or less nanocrystalline structure. Indexed (100)/(002) planes and preferential [100]/[002] growth are reported; no explicit polymorph name, unit-cell constants or coordinates are provided here.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 1 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Hydrophilic interface is the proposed advantage
intuition.text: Quaternary pyridinium salts render the otherwise hydrophobic conjugated polymers water-soluble. The authors argue that compatible hydrophilic surfaces improve sensitizer contact with CdS. The measured bare-film water contact angle is about 15 degrees; the introduction’s less-than-10-degree statement is a general background description, not this measured value.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Introduction, Figure 1d and polymer discussion

intuition.title: Carboxyl functionality and cell response
intuition.text: LM 3 has greater measured adsorption than LM 2 and higher reported cell efficiency. The authors attribute this to carboxyl-mediated electronic coupling and improved electron transfer. This is their interpretation; adsorption density, optical tail and cell performance are retained as distinct evidence, not direct structural proof of a particular surface bond.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure 3, Figure 4 and Table I

intuition.title: Energy conventions remain as printed
intuition.text: The source gives positive LUMO values of 3.23 and 3.42 eV with normal hydrogen electrode for LM 2/LM 3, and a CdS conduction-band value of 4.2 eV in its interpretation. The underlying CV curves are not shown. The values are not converted to vacuum energies, sign-corrected or treated as new measured CdS band levels.

intuition.title: Distinct structural dimensions
intuition.text: The authors report approximately 7 ± 1 nm CdS particles, approximately 20 nm sharp-edged aggregates, approximately 8.2 nm Scherrer grains and approximately 150 nm film thickness. These describe different objects and are not interchangeable. The statistic represented by ±1 nm is not identified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Film preparation, Figure 1 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Crystallinity is qualified
intuition.text: SAED has diffuse rings, which the authors associate with significant amorphous and/or less nanocrystalline structure. Indexed (100)/(002) planes and preferential [100]/[002] growth are reported; no explicit polymorph name, unit-cell constants or coordinates are provided here.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 1 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Hydrophilic interface is the proposed advantage
intuition.text: Quaternary pyridinium salts render the otherwise hydrophobic conjugated polymers water-soluble. The authors argue that compatible hydrophilic surfaces improve sensitizer contact with CdS. The measured bare-film water contact angle is about 15 degrees; the introduction’s less-than-10-degree statement is a general background description, not this measured value.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Introduction, Figure 1d and polymer discussion

intuition.title: Carboxyl functionality and cell response
intuition.text: LM 3 has greater measured adsorption than LM 2 and higher reported cell efficiency. The authors attribute this to carboxyl-mediated electronic coupling and improved electron transfer. This is their interpretation; adsorption density, optical tail and cell performance are retained as distinct evidence, not direct structural proof of a particular surface bond.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure 3, Figure 4 and Table I

intuition.title: Energy conventions remain as printed
intuition.text: The source gives positive LUMO values of 3.23 and 3.42 eV with normal hydrogen electrode for LM 2/LM 3, and a CdS conduction-band value of 4.2 eV in its interpretation. The underlying CV curves are not shown. The values are not converted to vacuum energies, sign-corrected or treated as new measured CdS band levels.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Energy-level discussion

intuition.title: Before-treatment evidence is not a final-product result
intuition.text: Figures 1–3 panels a, b show water/ethanol precursors before solvothermal treatment: yellow aqueous colloid or straw-yellow ethanol precipitate, mainly amorphous. Panels c–i are after treatment. Precursor FTIR 900 cm−1 signal is assigned to the aqueous peroxo group; absence/persistence wording does not quantify an exact residual concentration.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 2–4, Figures 1–3; Sections 3.1–3.2

intuition.title: Labeled table mapping retains the contradictory prose order
intuition.text: Table 1 explicitly assigns each TEM/XRD/area/zeta/activity value to TW, TWE4, TWE1, TWE0.25, TE. The preceding Figure 2 e–i order and prose Scherrer list conflict. The table assignment remains explicit alongside that conflict; the narrative 9.0 nm endpoint does not replace Table 1 9.7 nm.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 3–4, Section 3.1 and Table 1

intuition.title: Lengths, widths, particles and crystallites remain separate
intuition.text: TW is described as rods about 80×7 nm; TE as rectangles about 26×14 nm. Table 1 DTEM 80.6 and 26.1 nm are source diameter metrics, whereas 13.4 and 11.8 nm are Scherrer crystallite estimates. HRTEM 3.4/4.8 Å source assignments are retained literally and do not establish a measured unit-cell model.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 3–4, Figures 3–4 and Table 1

intuition.title: Poor solvent controls are not omitted or promoted to successes
intuition.text: Pure n-propanol and n-butanol yield poorly crystalline aggregated material with amorphous floccus-like morphology. They share the explicit method but have no assigned numeric size or catalytic result and were excluded from the photocatalysis study.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 2–3, Sections 2.4 and 3.1–3.2

intuition.title: Catalytic outcome belongs to an additionally dried specimen
intuition.text: Catalysts were rotary-evaporated 45°C then dried 110°C 1 h. The assay uses 10 mg/L phenol, 1 g/L TiO2, 75 mL in an 80 mL tube, dark 30 min, 365 nm 16 W UV with stirring. Table 1 contains 6 h efficiencies. The no-catalyst blank and catechol explanation stay qualitative; curves were not digitized.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 2–5, Section 2.4, Section 3.3, Figure 5 and Table 1

intuition.title: Growth mechanism remains an attributed interpretation
intuition.text: Equation 2 proposes peroxotitanate condensation and growth units; Scheme 1 attributes anisotropy to solvent/facet interactions. The scheme expressly does not depict real crystal lengths. Literature pH 3–9, methanol and 2-propanol discussions are explanatory context, not added experimental conditions or reagents for these recipes.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 4–5, Section 3.4, Equation 2 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Poor solvent controls are not omitted or promoted to successes

intuition.title: Catalytic outcome belongs to an additionally dried specimen
intuition.text: Catalysts were rotary-evaporated 45°C then dried 110°C 1 h. The assay uses 10 mg/L phenol, 1 g/L TiO2, 75 mL in an 80 mL tube, dark 30 min, 365 nm 16 W UV with stirring. intuition.title: Growth mechanism remains an attributed interpretation

Unknown volumes, ramps and pressure remain unknown.
intuition.source_locator: Main p. 2, Sections 2.1–2.2

intuition.title: Before-treatment evidence is not a final-product result
intuition.text: Figures 1–3 panels a, b show water/ethanol precursors before solvothermal treatment: yellow aqueous colloid or straw-yellow ethanol precipitate, mainly amorphous. Panels c–i are after treatment. Precursor FTIR 900 cm−1 signal is assigned to the aqueous peroxo group; absence/persistence wording does not quantify an exact residual concentration.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 2–4, Figures 1–3; Sections 3.1–3.2

intuition.title: Labeled table mapping retains the contradictory prose order
intuition.text: Table 1 explicitly assigns each TEM/XRD/area/zeta/activity value to TW, TWE4, TWE1, TWE0.25, TE. The preceding Figure 2 e–i order and prose Scherrer list conflict. The table assignment remains explicit alongside that conflict; the narrative 9.0 nm endpoint does not replace Table 1 9.7 nm.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 3–4, Section 3.1 and Table 1

intuition.title: Lengths, widths, particles and crystallites remain separate
intuition.text: TW is described as rods about 80×7 nm; TE as rectangles about 26×14 nm. Table 1 DTEM 80.6 and 26.1 nm are source diameter metrics, whereas 13.4 and 11.8 nm are Scherrer crystallite estimates. HRTEM 3.4/4.8 Å source assignments are retained literally and do not establish a measured unit-cell model.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 3–4, Figures 3–4 and Table 1

intuition.title: Poor solvent controls are not omitted or promoted to successes
intuition.text: Pure n-propanol and n-butanol yield poorly crystalline aggregated material with amorphous floccus-like morphology. They share the explicit method but have no assigned numeric size or catalytic result and were excluded from the photocatalysis study.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 2–3, Sections 2.4 and 3.1–3.2

intuition.title: Catalytic outcome belongs to an additionally dried specimen
intuition.text: Catalysts were rotary-evaporated 45°C then dried 110°C 1 h. The assay uses 10 mg/L phenol, 1 g/L TiO2, 75 mL in an 80 mL tube, dark 30 min, 365 nm 16 W UV with stirring. Table 1 contains 6 h efficiencies. The no-catalyst blank and catechol explanation stay qualitative; curves were not digitized.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 2–5, Section 2.4, Section 3.3, Figure 5 and Table 1

intuition.title: Growth mechanism remains an attributed interpretation
intuition.text: Equation 2 proposes peroxotitanate condensation and growth units; Scheme 1 attributes anisotropy to solvent/facet interactions. The scheme expressly does not depict real crystal lengths. Literature pH 3–9, methanol and 2-propanol discussions are explanatory context, not added experimental conditions or reagents for these recipes.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 4–5, Section 3.4, Equation 2 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Shared precursor preparation, distinct solvent conditions
intuition.text: Every final solvent route retains the stated 6 g Ti(SO4)2, 0.2 M solution, 3 M ammonia to pH 7.5, 20 h aging, filtrate conductivity strictly below 100 μs/cm, 125 mL selected solvent, 0.5 h ultrasound, 2.5 mL 30 wt% H2O2 in an ice bath, 78°C 4 h reflux and 120°C 15 h solvothermal treatment. Unknown volumes, ramps and pressure remain unknown.
intuition.source_locator: Main p. 2, Sections 2.1–2.2

intuition.title: Before-treatment evidence is not a final-product result
intuition.text: Figures 1–3 panels a, b show water/ethanol precursors before solvothermal treatment: yellow aqueous colloid or straw-yellow ethanol precipitate, mainly amorphous. Panels c–i are after treatment. Precursor FTIR 900 cm−1 signal is assigned to the aqueous peroxo group; absence/persistence wording does not quantify an exact residual concentration.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 2–4, Figures 1–3; Sections 3.1–3.2

intuition.title: Labeled table mapping retains the contradictory prose order
intuition.text: Table 1 explicitly assigns each TEM/XRD/area/zeta/activity value to TW, TWE4, TWE1, TWE0.25, TE. The preceding Figure 2 e–i order and prose Scherrer list conflict. The table assignment remains explicit alongside that conflict; the narrative 9.0 nm endpoint does not replace Table 1 9.7 nm.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 3–4, Section 3.1 and Table 1

intuition.title: Lengths, widths, particles and crystallites remain separate
intuition.text: TW is described as rods about 80×7 nm; TE as rectangles about 26×14 nm. Table 1 DTEM 80.6 and 26.1 nm are source diameter metrics, whereas 13.4 and 11.8 nm are Scherrer crystallite estimates. HRTEM 3.4/4.8 Å source assignments are retained literally and do not establish a measured unit-cell model.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 3–4, Figures 3–4 and Table 1

intuition.title: Poor solvent controls are not omitted or promoted to successes
intuition.text: Pure n-propanol and n-butanol yield poorly crystalline aggregated material with amorphous floccus-like morphology. They share the explicit method but have no assigned numeric size or catalytic result and were excluded from the photocatalysis study.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 2–3, Sections 2.4 and 3.1–3.2

intuition.title: Catalytic outcome belongs to an additionally dried specimen
intuition.text: Catalysts were rotary-evaporated 45°C then dried 110°C 1 h. The assay uses 10 mg/L phenol, 1 g/L TiO2, 75 mL in an 80 mL tube, dark 30 min, 365 nm 16 W UV with stirring. Table 1 contains 6 h efficiencies. The no-catalyst blank and catechol explanation stay qualitative; curves were not digitized.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 2–5, Section 2.4, Section 3.3, Figure 5 and Table 1

intuition.title: Growth mechanism remains an attributed interpretation
intuition.text: Equation 2 proposes peroxotitanate condensation and growth units; Scheme 1 attributes anisotropy to solvent/facet interactions. The scheme expressly does not depict real crystal lengths. Literature pH 3–9, methanol and 2-propanol discussions are explanatory context, not added experimental conditions or reagents for these recipes.
intuition.source_locator: Main pp. 4–5, Section 3.4, Equation 2 and Scheme 1

intuition.title: Lengths, widths, particles and crystallites remain separate

intuition.title: Combustion and crystallization are distinct stages
intuition.text: The 650 °C, 30 min air treatment produces a gray, amorphous combustion body. The brief 1150 °C, 90 s air treatment produces the yellow crystalline YAG:Ce body. The reported 18 nm Scherrer domain size belongs to the final product, not the amorphous intermediate. Above 1150 °C or at longer times the authors report larger grains and more sintering; below 1000 °C they report amorphous white, nonluminescent samples. No discrete comparison times or full schedules are given.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Synthesis and thermal comparison

intuition.title: Clusters, crystallites and surface-linked molecules
intuition.text: Grinding and sonic-bath treatment yield 100–1000 nm clusters made from an interconnected network of approximately 20 nm nanocrystals by TEM/HRTEM. These scales are distinct from the 18 nm XRD coherent-domain estimate. Glycine is proposed to bridge the YAG:Ce surface and TRITC through its carboxylic and primary-amine groups; this is not an experimentally determined surface molecular structure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Figure 2 and conjugation discussion

intuition.title: Energy transfer is inferred from spectra and decay
intuition.text: At 440 nm excitation, TRITC absorbs weakly but conjugate emission is dominated by the dye. The conjugate also shows faster Ce emission decay monitored at 520 nm. The authors infer predominantly nonradiative dipole–dipole energy transfer and estimate an average rate of approximately 10^8–10^9 s−1; donor–acceptor distances and size polydispersity prevent a precise quantitative rate distribution. The 60 ns host time is defined at intensity 1/e, rather than a fitted universal lifetime.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figures 3–4 and energy-transfer discussion

intuition.title: The shell is an explanatory distance model
intuition.text: The source estimates a critical transfer distance of approximately 7 nm using Förster–Dexter theory. A modeled outer 5 nm shell of an 18 nm YAG:Ce crystal places more than 90% of Ce ions within transfer distance of the surface. This is a statistical energy-transfer picture, not a measured core–shell particle or compositional map.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Equation and following paragraph

intuition.title: Photobleaching probes the dye contribution
intuition.text: After 65 h irradiation at 300 nm from a 450 W xenon lamp, the conjugate becomes slightly yellow and the dye spectral contribution falls. Bleaching is incomplete; the authors suggest strong scattering limits light penetration. The remaining fast decay has a smaller contribution. No new numerical post-bleach lifetime or particle structure is reported.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Figure 5 and photobleaching discussion

intuition.title: Alternative fuels and a negative dye control
intuition.text: Urea and citric acid are separate fuel alternatives reported to yield 23 nm crystals with lower quantum yield and more sintering. Their complete recipes are not supplied. A separate glycine/Rhodamine B treatment does not produce a dye–nanocrystal conjugate; its amounts and workup are not independently specified and are not filled from the TRITC recipe.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Alternative fuels and Rhodamine B control

intuition.title: Combustion and crystallization are distinct stages
intuition.text: The 650 °C, 30 min air treatment produces a gray, amorphous combustion body. The brief 1150 °C, 90 s air treatment produces the yellow crystalline YAG:Ce body. The reported 18 nm Scherrer domain size belongs to the final product, not the amorphous intermediate. Above 1150 °C or at longer times the authors report larger grains and more sintering; below 1000 °C they report amorphous white, nonluminescent samples. No discrete comparison times or full schedules are given.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Synthesis and thermal comparison

intuition.title: Clusters, crystallites and surface-linked molecules
intuition.text: Grinding and sonic-bath treatment yield 100–1000 nm clusters made from an interconnected network of approximately 20 nm nanocrystals by TEM/HRTEM. These scales are distinct from the 18 nm XRD coherent-domain estimate. Glycine is proposed to bridge the YAG:Ce surface and TRITC through its carboxylic and primary-amine groups; this is not an experimentally determined surface molecular structure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Figure 2 and conjugation discussion

intuition.title: Energy transfer is inferred from spectra and decay
intuition.text: At 440 nm excitation, TRITC absorbs weakly but conjugate emission is dominated by the dye. The conjugate also shows faster Ce emission decay monitored at 520 nm. The authors infer predominantly nonradiative dipole–dipole energy transfer and estimate an average rate of approximately 10^8–10^9 s−1; donor–acceptor distances and size polydispersity prevent a precise quantitative rate distribution. The 60 ns host time is defined at intensity 1/e, rather than a fitted universal lifetime.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figures 3–4 and energy-transfer discussion

intuition.title: The shell is an explanatory distance model
intuition.text: The source estimates a critical transfer distance of approximately 7 nm using Förster–Dexter theory. A modeled outer 5 nm shell of an 18 nm YAG:Ce crystal places more than 90% of Ce ions within transfer distance of the surface. This is a statistical energy-transfer picture, not a measured core–shell particle or compositional map.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Equation and following paragraph

intuition.title: Photobleaching probes the dye contribution
intuition.text: After 65 h irradiation at 300 nm from a 450 W xenon lamp, the conjugate becomes slightly yellow and the dye spectral contribution falls. Bleaching is incomplete; the authors suggest strong scattering limits light penetration. The remaining fast decay has a smaller contribution. No new numerical post-bleach lifetime or particle structure is reported.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Figure 5 and photobleaching discussion

intuition.title: Alternative fuels and a negative dye control
intuition.text: Urea and citric acid are separate fuel alternatives reported to yield 23 nm crystals with lower quantum yield and more sintering. Their complete recipes are not supplied. A separate glycine/Rhodamine B treatment does not produce a dye–nanocrystal conjugate; its amounts and workup are not independently specified and are not filled from the TRITC recipe.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Alternative fuels and Rhodamine B control

intuition.title: Temperature cycling and the comparison routes
intuition.text: The authors cool the reaction after injection to 80 °C and then reheat to 370 °C. They report teardrop CdSe cores and asymmetric head–tail CdSe/CdS rods. Separate constant-370 °C preparations are described as symmetric rods with single emission spectra, but their charges and dwell times are not separately specified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, Sections 2.3 and 3; Figure 4

intuition.title: The larger-seed TOP omission is a separate recipe option
intuition.text: The core method states that the separate 1.5 mL TOP addition is omitted for large-size seeds. This does not remove the 1.5 mL TOP used with selenium. No numerical dimension or displayed specimen is explicitly assigned to that variant, so the Figure 2(a) dimensions remain with the representative cycled-core route.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.3.1

intuition.title: Particle dimensions do not locate an internal interface
intuition.text: TEM gives core dimensions 10.5 ± 0.7 nm by 6.4 ± 0.4 nm, with aspect ratio 1.7 ± 0.1. For CdSe/CdS rods, the thicker head/stem is 18.3 ± 1.8 nm by 7.7 ± 0.8 nm, with aspect ratio 2.4 ± 0.3; the total length is 44.8 ± 4.1 nm. The authors propose that the head contains the CdSe core. The images do not supply a measured internal interface or shell-thickness map. Approximately 70% are classified as head–tail rods.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 2 and discussion

intuition.title: Double emission is not proof of two size populations
intuition.text: The purified cores show approximate absorption features at 633 and 580 nm and PL peaks at 582 and 649 nm. No clear bimodal TEM size distribution is observed. After CdS growth the emission peaks shift to about 622 and 663 nm; relative quantum yield rises from about 3% to about 38%. The authors connect the optical behavior to varied faceting or morphology, without resolving separate particle populations.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figure 1 and discussion

intuition.title: Wurtzite assignment and the growth model
intuition.text: Powder XRD assigns both cycled products to wurtzite. The source identifies reflections at 35° and 46° as characteristic CdSe <102> and <103>, and describes stronger relative <002> intensity for elongated particles. A shift from bulk CdSe toward CdS is interpreted as shell growth; no numerical refined lattice constant is supplied. The proposed mechanism invokes ligand-limited growth during cooling and renewed anisotropic growth on reheating.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figures 3 and 4

intuition.title: Two source schematic labels remain unresolved
intuition.text: Figure 4 labels growth <001>, whereas the prose discusses <002>. Its cycle label is 80–370–80 °C, whereas the method records the initial injection, cooling to 80 °C, reheating to 370 °C and room-temperature workup. These are retained as source differences; no silently corrected crystal direction or final 80 °C hold is imposed. The 10 min final anneal is explicit in the core discussion, not independently repeated in the shell procedure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, Section 2.3, Section 3 and Figure 4

intuition.text: The authors cool the reaction after injection to 80 °C and then reheat to 370 °C. They report teardrop CdSe cores and asymmetric head–tail CdSe/CdS rods. Separate constant-370 °C preparations are described as symmetric rods with single emission spectra, but their charges and dwell times are not separately specified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, Sections 2.3 and 3; Figure 4

intuition.title: The larger-seed TOP omission is a separate recipe option
intuition.text: The core method states that the separate 1.5 mL TOP addition is omitted for large-size seeds. This does not remove the 1.5 mL TOP used with selenium. No numerical dimension or displayed specimen is explicitly assigned to that variant, so the Figure 2(a) dimensions remain with the representative cycled-core route.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Section 2.3.1

intuition.title: Particle dimensions do not locate an internal interface
intuition.text: TEM gives core dimensions 10.5 ± 0.7 nm by 6.4 ± 0.4 nm, with aspect ratio 1.7 ± 0.1. For CdSe/CdS rods, the thicker head/stem is 18.3 ± 1.8 nm by 7.7 ± 0.8 nm, with aspect ratio 2.4 ± 0.3; the total length is 44.8 ± 4.1 nm. The authors propose that the head contains the CdSe core. The images do not supply a measured internal interface or shell-thickness map. Approximately 70% are classified as head–tail rods.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 2 and discussion

intuition.title: Double emission is not proof of two size populations
intuition.text: The purified cores show approximate absorption features at 633 and 580 nm and PL peaks at 582 and 649 nm. No clear bimodal TEM size distribution is observed. After CdS growth the emission peaks shift to about 622 and 663 nm; relative quantum yield rises from about 3% to about 38%. The authors connect the optical behavior to varied faceting or morphology, without resolving separate particle populations.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figure 1 and discussion

intuition.title: Wurtzite assignment and the growth model
intuition.text: Powder XRD assigns both cycled products to wurtzite. The source identifies reflections at 35° and 46° as characteristic CdSe <102> and <103>, and describes stronger relative <002> intensity for elongated particles. A shift from bulk CdSe toward CdS is interpreted as shell growth; no numerical refined lattice constant is supplied. The proposed mechanism invokes ligand-limited growth during cooling and renewed anisotropic growth on reheating.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figures 3 and 4

intuition.title: Two source schematic labels remain unresolved
intuition.text: Figure 4 labels growth <001>, whereas the prose discusses <002>. Its cycle label is 80–370–80 °C, whereas the method records the initial injection, cooling to 80 °C, reheating to 370 °C and room-temperature workup. These are retained as source differences; no silently corrected crystal direction or final 80 °C hold is imposed. The 10 min final anneal is explicit in the core discussion, not independently repeated in the shell procedure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, Section 2.3, Section 3 and Figure 4

intuition.title: Study context: Precursor chemistry and distinct synthesis controls
intuition.text: Aminoarsine is conditioned with oleylamine at 40 °C until bubbling stops, consistent with source-proposed transamination. Exact reacted molecular species is unknown. The quantified 1 mmol cyanoborohydride recipe gives pure InAs; the 0.5 mmol and 3/6 mmol comparisons are distinct incompletely specified observations. Excess reductant promotes metallic In, while NaCl is a washing-dependent by-product.
intuition.source_locator: Supporting Information PDF p. 3,13, Sections 1.2.1–1.2.2, 2.1 and Figure S2

intuition.title: Study context: Washing comparison does not overwrite the reported recipe
intuition.text: The typical recipe explicitly uses a first toluene/methanol/isopropanol wash and two later toluene/ethanol washes, each centrifuged at 4500 rpm for 10 min. Figure S2b compares ethanol versus methanol purification and reports NaCl removal using methanol. Complete alternative volumes and sequence are not supplied, so the observation is preserved separately.
intuition.source_locator: Supporting Information PDF p. 4,13, Workup and Figure S2b

intuition.title: Study context: Parent QDs and ligand-exchanged QDs are separate samples
intuition.text: Pristine oleylamine-capped InAs has a reported 2.2 nm TEM mean and In/As ratio 1.04. After exchange, the source reports retained phase, morphology and absorption, decreased interparticle distance, loss of N 1s, S 2p near 163 eV and In/As 1.13. It does not report a newly measured 2.2 nm mean for the exchanged sample.
intuition.source_locator: Supporting Information PDF p. 14–15,26–27, Figures S3 and S12

intuition.title: Study context: Surface chemistry is not bulk phase purity
intuition.text: Pristine XRD is consistent with zinc-blende InAs, while XPS shows about 3 at% surface oxygen and a weak As(III)-consistent contribution. A phase-pure diffraction pattern does not establish an oxygen-free surface. The ICSD patterns are references, not refined specimen atomic coordinates.
intuition.source_locator: Supporting Information PDF p. 14–15, Section 2.2 and Figure S3

intuition.title: Study context: Electrode fabrication and flooding are source-specific contexts
intuition.text: Native oleylamine-capped QDs are deposited from toluene with a later Nafion layer for H-cell tests. Exchanged QDs are deposited from ethanol with a mixed binder ink for flow-cell tests. Source observations associate residual oleylamine with loss of support hydrophobicity; the mechanism is proposed, and no contact angle is measured or inferred from the droplet photograph.
intuition.source_locator: Supporting Information PDF p. 5–6,25–26, Electrode crafting and Figure S11

intuition.title: Study context: Catalytic metrics belong to the electrode and testing regime
intuition.text: Near-unity formate Faradaic efficiency is the flow-cell result for exchanged-QD electrodes in 1 M KOH. The native-ligand H-cell in 1 M KHCO3 peaks near 55% at −5 mA/cm2. These are not properties of an isolated pristine particle or claims of complete electrochemical parameter coverage. Main-figure captions retain one-hour chronopotentiometry and their controls.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, Figures 1–3 and catalytic discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Reconstruction and active phase are distinct kinds of evidence
intuition.text: Post-electrolysis STEM/EDS indicates In-rich agglomerates and partially oxidized InAs1−x; ex-situ XPS is In-rich and As-depleted with predominantly In2O3. Metallic indium as the operative active phase is the authors’ interpretation of electrochemistry, not the same claim as the ex-situ oxide signal. Detailed SI post-electrolysis specimen comparisons are outside the selected pages.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Post-electrolysis discussion

intuition.title: Study context: Parent QDs and ligand-exchanged QDs are separate samples

intuition.title: Sulfur ratio selects oxide, mixed phase or disulfide
intuition.text: Under the reported 300 °C, 12 h solvothermal conditions, Table 1 and Figure 1 assign MoO2 to the no-sulfur feed, MoO2 + MoS2 to MoO3:S = 1:1, and MoS2 to 1:2 and 1:3. The typical 1:2 feed contains 0.576 g (4 mmol) MoO3 and 8 mmol sulfur; the printed sulfur number 0.256 lacks a mass unit. Other ratios do not establish their own absolute precursor charges.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–3, Preparation, Figure 1 and Table 1

intuition.title: Phase identification and composition remain distinct
intuition.text: The two sulfur-rich products are indexed as 2H-MoS2, space group P63/mmc (194), with (002), (100), (103) and (110) reflections. Chemical analysis reports MoS1.99 for 1:2 and MoS2.02 for 1:3. These are chemical-analysis compositions, not refined site occupancies or a measure of interfacial geometry.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, XRD and chemical-analysis discussion

intuition.title: Study-wide dimensions are not two separately measured batches
intuition.text: The paper reports refined a = 3.16 Å and c = 12.40 Å and describes thin platelets around 100 nm. Figure 2b is an individual particle about 200 nm across. The text does not uniquely map those observations to ratio c or d; the individual particle is not a second population mean. Reference-card values a0 = 3.1616 Å and c0 = 12.2985 Å are literature comparison data, not new measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, XRD refinement paragraph and Figure 2

intuition.title: IR supports the authors’ no-intercalation interpretation
intuition.text: The prose assigns an IR band at 382 cm⁻¹; Figure 3 labels 382.8. The reported absence of bands from 500 to 4000 cm⁻¹ is interpreted by the authors as no guest pyridine between the MoS2 layers. This is their spectral interpretation, not a quantitative limit on every possible impurity. The analyzed ratio-specific batch is not identified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 3 and IR discussion

intuition.title: The proposed MoO2 intermediate
intuition.text: The authors propose reduction of MoO3 to MoO2 by hydrazine, followed by sulfidation to MoS2. Adding sufficient sulfur to the mixed 1:1 product and replacing MoO3 with MoO2 are reported to yield MoS2, but those supporting tests lack separate charge and schedule details. Equations 1 and 2 are proposed reaction steps, not measured transient concentrations.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Mechanistic discussion and equations 1–2

intuition.title: Temperature limits and solvent role
intuition.text: Below 250 °C the reaction requires a long time; above 350 °C pyridine may decompose without greatly improving MoS2 crystallinity. Exact temperature series and durations are not supplied. The authors choose 300 °C for 12 h and describe pyridine as heat-stable at the chosen conditions, sulfur-solubilizing and miscible with hydrazine. Lubrication suitability is a proposed application; no functional performance test is reported.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Temperature discussion and conclusion

intuition.title: Sulfur ratio selects oxide, mixed phase or disulfide
intuition.text: Under the reported 300 °C, 12 h solvothermal conditions, Table 1 and Figure 1 assign MoO2 to the no-sulfur feed, MoO2 + MoS2 to MoO3:S = 1:1, and MoS2 to 1:2 and 1:3. The typical 1:2 feed contains 0.576 g (4 mmol) MoO3 and 8 mmol sulfur; the printed sulfur number 0.256 lacks a mass unit. Other ratios do not establish their own absolute precursor charges.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–3, Preparation, Figure 1 and Table 1

intuition.title: Phase identification and composition remain distinct
intuition.text: The two sulfur-rich products are indexed as 2H-MoS2, space group P63/mmc (194), with (002), (100), (103) and (110) reflections. Chemical analysis reports MoS1.99 for 1:2 and MoS2.02 for 1:3. These are chemical-analysis compositions, not refined site occupancies or a measure of interfacial geometry.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, XRD and chemical-analysis discussion

intuition.title: Study-wide dimensions are not two separately measured batches
intuition.text: The paper reports refined a = 3.16 Å and c = 12.40 Å and describes thin platelets around 100 nm. Figure 2b is an individual particle about 200 nm across. The text does not uniquely map those observations to ratio c or d; the individual particle is not a second population mean. Reference-card values a0 = 3.1616 Å and c0 = 12.2985 Å are literature comparison data, not new measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, XRD refinement paragraph and Figure 2

intuition.title: IR supports the authors’ no-intercalation interpretation
intuition.text: The prose assigns an IR band at 382 cm⁻¹; Figure 3 labels 382.8. The reported absence of bands from 500 to 4000 cm⁻¹ is interpreted by the authors as no guest pyridine between the MoS2 layers. This is their spectral interpretation, not a quantitative limit on every possible impurity. The analyzed ratio-specific batch is not identified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 3 and IR discussion

intuition.title: The proposed MoO2 intermediate
intuition.text: The authors propose reduction of MoO3 to MoO2 by hydrazine, followed by sulfidation to MoS2. Adding sufficient sulfur to the mixed 1:1 product and replacing MoO3 with MoO2 are reported to yield MoS2, but those supporting tests lack separate charge and schedule details. Equations 1 and 2 are proposed reaction steps, not measured transient concentrations.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Mechanistic discussion and equations 1–2

intuition.title: Temperature limits and solvent role
intuition.text: Below 250 °C the reaction requires a long time; above 350 °C pyridine may decompose without greatly improving MoS2 crystallinity. Exact temperature series and durations are not supplied. The authors choose 300 °C for 12 h and describe pyridine as heat-stable at the chosen conditions, sulfur-solubilizing and miscible with hydrazine. Lubrication suitability is a proposed application; no functional performance test is reported.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Temperature discussion and conclusion

intuition.title: Sulfur ratio selects oxide, mixed phase or disulfide
intuition.text: Under the reported 300 °C, 12 h solvothermal conditions, Table 1 and Figure 1 assign MoO2 to the no-sulfur feed, MoO2 + MoS2 to MoO3:S = 1:1, and MoS2 to 1:2 and 1:3. The typical 1:2 feed contains 0.576 g (4 mmol) MoO3 and 8 mmol sulfur; the printed sulfur number 0.256 lacks a mass unit. Other ratios do not establish their own absolute precursor charges.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–3, Preparation, Figure 1 and Table 1

intuition.title: Phase identification and composition remain distinct
intuition.text: The two sulfur-rich products are indexed as 2H-MoS2, space group P63/mmc (194), with (002), (100), (103) and (110) reflections. Chemical analysis reports MoS1.99 for 1:2 and MoS2.02 for 1:3. These are chemical-analysis compositions, not refined site occupancies or a measure of interfacial geometry.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, XRD and chemical-analysis discussion

intuition.title: Study-wide dimensions are not two separately measured batches
intuition.text: The paper reports refined a = 3.16 Å and c = 12.40 Å and describes thin platelets around 100 nm. Figure 2b is an individual particle about 200 nm across. The text does not uniquely map those observations to ratio c or d; the individual particle is not a second population mean. Reference-card values a0 = 3.1616 Å and c0 = 12.2985 Å are literature comparison data, not new measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, XRD refinement paragraph and Figure 2

intuition.title: IR supports the authors’ no-intercalation interpretation
intuition.text: The prose assigns an IR band at 382 cm⁻¹; Figure 3 labels 382.8. The reported absence of bands from 500 to 4000 cm⁻¹ is interpreted by the authors as no guest pyridine between the MoS2 layers. This is their spectral interpretation, not a quantitative limit on every possible impurity. The analyzed ratio-specific batch is not identified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 3 and IR discussion

intuition.title: The proposed MoO2 intermediate
intuition.text: The authors propose reduction of MoO3 to MoO2 by hydrazine, followed by sulfidation to MoS2. Adding sufficient sulfur to the mixed 1:1 product and replacing MoO3 with MoO2 are reported to yield MoS2, but those supporting tests lack separate charge and schedule details. Equations 1 and 2 are proposed reaction steps, not measured transient concentrations.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Mechanistic discussion and equations 1–2

intuition.title: Temperature limits and solvent role
intuition.text: Below 250 °C the reaction requires a long time; above 350 °C pyridine may decompose without greatly improving MoS2 crystallinity. Exact temperature series and durations are not supplied. The authors choose 300 °C for 12 h and describe pyridine as heat-stable at the chosen conditions, sulfur-solubilizing and miscible with hydrazine. Lubrication suitability is a proposed application; no functional performance test is reported.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Temperature discussion and conclusion

intuition.title: Two concentrations and two composition bases
intuition.text: The target is 8 mol% Sc2O3-stabilized zirconia on an oxide basis. The method separately prints nominal starting values of 92 mol% ZrO(NO3)2 and 16 mol% Sc(NO3)3. Those literal feed values are not two normalized percentages summing to 100, nor an 8 mol% scandium-cation fraction. Total cation concentration is separate from urea concentration. The stock solvent and individual nitrate charges are not specified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, Experimental Procedure

intuition.title: Aging changes phase formation
intuition.text: The authors attribute the low-temperature stage to slow urea hydrolysis and homogeneous co-precipitation before crystallization at 180 °C. They propose polymeric/hydrous-oxide intermediates and a more ordered precursor; these are mechanistic interpretations, not measured transient species or molecular structures. Direct 180 °C treatment gives more monoclinic phase.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Results and Discussion; Figure 2

intuition.title: The 0.5 mol/L boundary remains unresolved
intuition.text: The first-page discussion describes pure cubic material for urea ≤0.5 mol/L. The conclusion uses <0.5 mol/L, and Figure 2a shows a small nonzero monoclinic point at 0.5 mol/L. The 0.5 mol/L route therefore retains an unresolved phase-purity boundary rather than a blanket pure-cubic label or an invented exact fraction.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–3, Results, Figure 2a and Conclusions

intuition.title: The short concentration series is a separate schedule
intuition.text: Figure 3 uses 80 °C for 24 h followed by 180 °C for 48 h, at 0.05, 0.1, 0.25 and 0.5 mol/L total cations with cation:urea = 1:4. The long urea series uses 48 h followed by 72 h. The 0.5 mol/L cation endpoint with that ratio is not silently reconciled with the general 0.1–1.5 mol/L urea range. Individual phase fractions for Figure 3 are not tabulated.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Experimental Procedure and Figure 3

intuition.title: Three size estimates describe different observables
intuition.text: For 0.05 mol/L cations and 0.2 mol/L urea after the long schedule, TEM gives an average grain size below 10 nm, XRD linewidth analysis gives 7.0 nm, and BET gives a specific surface area of 157 m²/g with an author-calculated equivalent size of 6 nm. These are separate analytical quantities, not repeated TEM diameters. Figure 5 shows a 50 nm scale bar.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 5 and morphology/XRD/BET paragraph

intuition.title: Calcination retains cubic phase while promoting grain growth
intuition.text: The paper reports cubic phase retention during 1 h calcination under stagnant air over 600–1200 °C. Grain size changes little below 800 °C and grows substantially above 1000 °C, reaching a text-reported XRD crystallite size of 36.5 nm at 1200 °C. Other Figure 6 point ordinates are preserved visually without extracting exact numbers.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 3, Experimental Procedure, calcination paragraph and Figure 6

intuition.title: Solution pH and applications are separate scopes
intuition.text: Figure 4 shows increasing final solution pH and decreasing XRD crystallite size as urea concentration rises. The plotted pH and size ordinates are not tabulated here. The paper motivates solid-oxide fuel-cell electrolytes through cited literature but supplies no conductivity measurement for these powders.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Introduction and Figure 4
